docs.title: oci-hermit
docs.text:
oci-hermit runs prebuilt OCI container images inside a small Linux virtual machine whose CPU is emulated in software (QEMU's TCG). It works on Windows, macOS and Linux as a normal user: no root, no admin rights, no hypervisor, no WSL and nothing to enable in the firmware. The commands follow Docker and Podman.

It is for people who need to test a container image on a machine where Docker and Podman are not an option, such as a locked-down company laptop. It is a development and testing tool, not a production runtime: it is slower than native, and the sandbox has no network at all.

Early days

oci-hermit is a pre-release (below 1.0). You can log in, pull, load, store and run images, in the foreground or detached, and exec into them today; published ports, bind mounts, pods and Compose are still to come. The roadmap says when, and the command-line reference lists every planned command with its issue.

docs.title: In 30 seconds
docs.text:
$ oci-hermit run public.ecr.aws/docker/library/debian:bookworm-slim sh -c 'uname -a; cat /etc/debian_version'
Unable to find image 'public.ecr.aws/docker/library/debian:bookworm-slim' locally
5b6c2c6cbc90: pulled (468 B)
2d66c782e484: pulled (28.1 MB)
Digest: sha256:ec8534cda2cb30f29f44f23e135297af7a1496f2990fd8e4e84aa36b081a757a
Linux (none) 6.18.63-oci-hermit-2 #1 SMP 2026-11-10 18:07:06 UTC aarch64 GNU/Linux
12.15

That pulled a Debian image on the host, checked every byte of it against its digest, booted a sandbox, ran the command in it and powered the sandbox off again, in about a second on a recent laptop. uname shows oci-hermit's own Linux kernel, whatever the host is. For a shell, add -it and run bash.

docs.title: What makes it different
docs.text:
• No elevated rights. It installs by unpacking a folder and runs as you. It installs no driver, service or network adapter. Running without admin rights says exactly what it needs.
  • No hardware virtualization. QEMU always runs with -accel tcg, so KVM, Hyper-V and Apple's Hypervisor framework are never used.
  • Sealed. The guest has no network device and no path out. Images are pulled by the host tool, never by the guest.
  • Both architectures everywhere. Because the CPU is emulated, amd64 and arm64 images run on any host.
  • Docker-style commands, with a few deliberate differences: see oci-hermit, Docker and Podman.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: oci-hermit is a Cargo workspace of three crates, plus the build scripts for the QEMU bundle and the guest kernel. How it works shows how the pieces fit at run time; this page maps them to the source.

docs.title: Crates and modules
docs.text: Path What it is crates/oci-hermit The host tool and its command line. crates/oci-hermit/src/cli.rs The command line (clap), modelled on Docker and Podman, including the commands that are not implemented yet. crates/oci-hermit/src/main.rs Dispatch; run (choose the architecture, find the image, attach its layer disks or build the initramfs, size the VM, run, report timings); machine info and machine boot. crates/oci-hermit/src/qemu.rs Finds the bundled QEMU ($OCI_HERMIT_QEMU_DIR, then the install layouts) and refuses any other: exact version and marker, tcg, firmware. crates/oci-hermit/src/guest.rs Finds each architecture's kernel, agent and crun ($OCI_HERMIT_GUEST_DIR/<arch>/{kernel,hermit-agent,crun}, then the install layouts). crates/oci-hermit/src/image.rs Reads an OCI image layout (directory or .tar): the manifest for the guest architecture, the config and the layers, checking every blob against its sha256 digest. crates/oci-hermit/src/store.rs The image store: one OCI layout in the user's data folder, images named by full reference and platform, a shared lock for readers and an exclusive one for deleting. crates/oci-hermit/src/registry.rs pull: the distribution API's reads over reqwest (rustls with ring, the OS trust store), with Basic and Bearer (token server) auth: Podman and Docker auth files and credential helpers, retries, $OCI_HERMIT_INSECURE_REGISTRIES. crates/oci-hermit/src/certs.rs Per-registry CA certificates and client certificates from the certs.d folders Podman and Docker use, or --cert-dir. crates/oci-hermit/src/reference.rs Image references as Docker reads them: debian is docker.io/library/debian:latest. crates/oci-hermit/src/load.rs load -i: OCI layouts and docker save archives (old and Docker 25+) into the store; unnamed images go by ID. crates/oci-hermit/src/containers.rs The container store: one folder per container in the user's data folder (container.json, state.json), names kept unique under a lock, and a lock held by the process running each container, so a crashed run is not shown as running; ps and rm. crates/oci-hermit/src/images.rs The image commands over the store: images, rmi, inspect, tag, save, image prune, image history, image exists, system df. crates/oci-hermit/src/erofs.rs Writes each layer as a read-only EROFS image without mounting anything, the way overlayfs reads a lower layer; cached by layer digest in the image store. crates/oci-hermit/src/rootfs.rs Applies layers in memory: whiteouts, opaque directories, hard links; refuses paths that climb out with ... crates/oci-hermit/src/users.rs Resolves the image's User (or -u) against the image's own /etc/passwd and /etc/group, as runc does. crates/oci-hermit/src/initramfs.rs Writes the guest initramfs (the agent as /init, /dev/console, the image under /rootfs) as a newc cpio in memory, without privileges. crates/oci-hermit/src/supervisor.rs Builds the QEMU command line, starts and supervises one sandbox VM, and drives the control protocol with timeouts. crates/hermit-agent The guest agent, PID 1 in the sandbox; Linux only. init.rs is the testable logic behind a System trait, including the container's OCI config.json; linux.rs the real system calls (nix): moving the root off the initramfs, running crun, receiving its terminal. It refuses to start anywhere but as PID 1 on Linux. guest/crun/build.sh Builds a static crun per guest architecture, with json-c, libseccomp and libcap, from pinned release tarballs. crates/hermit-proto The control protocol shared by host and agent: message types, the protocol version, and the Framer both sides use to cut the byte stream into lines of at most 64 KiB. qemu/ build.sh and patches for the TCG-only QEMU bundle. See Building QEMU. guest/kernel/ build.sh, config fragments and a boot test for the guest kernel. See Building the guest. docs/ This site. docs/design.md is the design document.

docs.title: Rules the code keeps
docs.text:
These come from the project's ground rules; a change that breaks one needs a design discussion first.

  • Nothing needs root, admin rights, a kernel driver or hardware virtualization. QEMU is always launched with -accel tcg.
  • The guest never gets egress. No change may open a path out of the sandbox without a design discussion.
  • Bind mounts are read-only unless :rw; published ports bind to 127.0.0.1. Both differ from Docker on purpose.
  • QEMU is GPL-2.0. It ships as a separate helper process and is never linked into a crate; deny.toml keeps GPL crates out.
  • No unsafe in host-side crates (unsafe_code = "deny" in the workspace lints).
  • The guest is untrusted. Cap line lengths, reject what is not a message, time out instead of blocking.
  • Every blob is verified against its digest when pulled, stored and read; a mismatch is an error, never a warning. Pulls happen in the host tool only.
  • PID 1 never exits or panics. The agent powers off instead, and anything it spawns resets the signal mask.

docs.title: Platform traps
docs.text:
Workarounds the code depends on. Each is commented where it lives.

Trap Where it is handled The qemu64 CPU stops the agent with SIGILL before any of its code runs: the static glibc uses AVX. supervisor::X86_64_CPU, an x86-64-v3 model. Without CONFIG_PCI=y, ACPI fails on microvm, userspace console writes fail with EIO and the guest looks hung (#54). guest/kernel/config/x86_64.config -run-with exit-with-parent=on stops QEMU from starting on Windows. Passed on POSIX hosts only; a kill-on-close Job Object (win32job) on Windows. On Windows, upstream QEMU's -chardev stdio drops piped input the guest cannot take yet, losing the host's first message. qemu/patches/0001-… Under TCG, the x86 guest's clock calibration fails on slow hosts, and microvm has no other timer (#61). qemu/patches/0002-… (a 1 GHz TSC) and tsc_early_khz=1000000; bundles older than oci-hermit-qemu-4 are refused. QEMU printing to stdout would corrupt the control channel. The console goes to a file; QEMU's stderr to qemu.log. A PID 1 that exits or panics panics the kernel; children inherit its blocked signals. The agent catches panics and powers off; spawned commands get a clean signal mask. A command must not keep root, but PID 1 needs root to power off. Around posix_spawn the agent switches its real and effective IDs to the user and keeps root as its saved IDs, then takes root back.

docs.title: Command-line reference
docs.text:
oci-hermit <COMMAND> [OPTIONS]

Every command takes -h or --help. oci-hermit --version (or -V) prints the version. The commands follow Docker and Podman; the deliberate differences are on their own page.

hrmt is the same program under a shorter name: every package has it beside oci-hermit (a symlink on Linux and macOS, a copy on Windows), and hrmt --help says hrmt. A hrmt link put elsewhere, such as ~/bin, still finds the qemu/ and guest/ folders beside the real file.

Command What it does run Run a command from an image in a new sandbox exec Run another command in a running container ps List containers logs Show a container's output stop Stop running containers kill Send a signal to running containers rm Remove containers pull Pull an image from a registry manifest inspect Show an image's platforms and digests in a registry, without pulling load Load images from a docker save archive or an OCI layout login Log in to a registry logout Remove a registry login images, image ls List stored images inspect, image inspect Show details of images as JSON tag, image tag Give an image another name save, image save Save images to an archive rmi, image rm Remove images image prune Remove unnamed images, or all of them image history Show the steps that built an image image exists Exit 0 if an image is stored, 1 if not system df Show how much space images use machine info, info Show what oci-hermit uses and where it keeps things machine boot Boot a sandbox until its agent is ready, then stop it version Print version information

Commands that are accepted but do nothing yet are listed under Planned commands.

docs.title: Images and names
docs.text:
Wherever a command takes an image, it takes:

  • a name: a full reference (docker.io/library/alpine:latest, ghcr.io/org/app:1.2) or one Docker would expand (alpine is docker.io/library/alpine:latest; mine/app:1 is docker.io/mine/app:1);
  • an image ID: the digest of the image's config, with or without sha256:, or a unique prefix of it (ab3f).

run also takes the path of an OCI layout directory or a .tar (an OCI archive or a docker save archive). A path that exists is read as a path, before any stored name.

docs.title: Platforms
docs.text: --platform names an image platform: linux/amd64 or linux/arm64. run and pull also accept the short forms amd64, arm64, x86_64 and aarch64. Without it, the host's platform is used. See Choose a platform.

docs.title: run
docs.text:
Run a command from an image in a new sandbox, and exit with the command's exit code.

oci-hermit run [OPTIONS] <IMAGE> [COMMAND]...
Argument or option Meaning IMAGE A name or ID in the store (pulled if it is not there), or the path of an OCI layout directory or .tar. COMMAND... The command and its arguments. Without one, the image's entrypoint and command run. Everything after IMAGE belongs to the command, including options. -i, --interactive Keep stdin open and pass it to the command. Without it, the command's stdin is closed at once. -t, --tty Give the command a terminal. With -i, an interactive shell. The terminal size is sent at the start; later resizes are not passed on yet. TERM is passed in from the host (xterm if unset) unless the image sets it. -u, --user <USER> Run as this user instead of the image's User: name, uid, name:group or uid:gid. Names are looked up in the image's /etc/passwd and /etc/group. --platform <PLATFORM> The image platform. Without it, the host's, or the other one with a warning if the image has only that. --cpus <CPUS> Number of emulated CPUs. Default 1. -m, --memory <MEMORY> Memory for the sandbox: a number with k, m or g (512m, 2g); bytes without a suffix, as Docker. At least 64m. Default: 512 MiB for a stored image, which runs from its layer disks; for an image run from a file, twice its size plus 256 MiB. --name <NAME> The container's name: a letter or digit, then letters, digits, _, . or -. Without one, a name such as quiet_nautilus is made up. A name stays taken until the container is removed. --rm Remove the container when the command ends. Without it the container is kept, exited, for ps -a, until rm. -d, --detach Run in the background: print the container's ID once its command started, and leave it running until it exits or is stopped. See logs and stop. With -i, its stdin stays open (nothing writes to it yet), so -dit … sh keeps a shell waiting. -p, --publish <PUBLISH> Planned (#27): [127.0.0.1:]HOST:CONTAINER, always bound to 127.0.0.1. Refused today. -v, --volume <VOLUME> Planned (#33): SRC:DST, with :ro or :rw; read-only by default. Refused today. --pod <POD> Planned (#35). Refused today.

The command runs in the image's working directory, with the image's environment, plus HOME from the user's /etc/passwd entry if the image does not set it.

Every run is recorded as a container (see ps), with its exit code, or with 125 and the reason if oci-hermit could not run it. Only the record and the output (see logs) are kept: the files the command changed are thrown away with the sandbox.

Each container's sandbox belongs to a small background oci-hermit process of its own, its monitor, which keeps QEMU, writes the output to the container's log and records how it ended. A run without -d stays attached to it: if that run goes away (the terminal closes, the process is killed), the monitor stops the container. With -d the container runs on after run returns. There is no daemon: nothing runs when no container does.

Ctrl-C at a run without -d is passed on to the container's command as SIGINT, and SIGTERM sent to run as SIGTERM, as docker run does (on Windows, Ctrl-C and Ctrl-Break). What happens then is up to the command. One that is PID 1 in its container, as every container's command is, ignores signals it has no handler for: sleep does, so Ctrl-C does not end run … sleep 60. Use oci-hermit stop or oci-hermit kill from another terminal. With -t, Ctrl-C goes to the container's terminal instead, as a keystroke.

$ oci-hermit run public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20 cat /etc/alpine-release
3.20.10
$ oci-hermit run -u nobody public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20 id
uid=65534(nobody) gid=65534(nobody)
$ oci-hermit run -d --name ticker public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20 sh -c 'while true; do date; sleep 5; done'
b472a05e48e7c828a74996b9a0c363491ec4e605b00c42ff03bf933847940407

oci-hermit run -it public.ecr.aws/docker/library/debian:bookworm-slim bash
oci-hermit run --platform linux/amd64 --cpus 2 -m 2g ./app.tar

Exit codes: the command's own exit code (128 plus the signal number if a signal ended it), or 125 when oci-hermit itself fails: the image cannot be found or read, a flag is refused, the sandbox does not boot, or the command cannot be started. With -d, 0 once the command started.

Windows: capture run -d's ID in a file, not with $(...)

On Windows, id=$(oci-hermit run -d …) does not return while the container runs: the container's monitor inherits the shell's output pipe (#105). Write the ID to a file instead (oci-hermit run -d … > ticker.id), or find it later with oci-hermit ps.

Set OCI_HERMIT_TIMINGS=1 to print how long each phase took, on stderr:

$ OCI_HERMIT_TIMINGS=1 oci-hermit run public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20 true
timings: prepare 0.04s, boot 0.33s, command 0.01s, stop 0.02s, total 0.41s

docs.title: exec
docs.text:
Run another command in a running container, beside its own: in the same filesystem (what the container wrote is there), processes, hostname and limits. Exits with the command's exit code.

oci-hermit exec [OPTIONS] <CONTAINER> <COMMAND>...
Option Meaning -i, --interactive Pass stdin to the command. Without it, the command's stdin is closed. -t, --tty Give the command a terminal (see run -t). -u, --user <USER> Run as this user instead of the container's: name, uid, name:group or uid:gid. Names are looked up in the image's /etc/passwd and /etc/group, as run -u does; a user added inside the running container is not seen yet, so use its number. -e, --env <NAME=value> Set an environment variable over the container's; -e NAME passes this shell's own value. Repeatable. -w, --workdir <DIR> Working directory; the container's by default. 
$ oci-hermit run -d --name web public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20 sleep 1d
$ oci-hermit exec web cat /etc/alpine-release
3.20.10
$ oci-hermit exec -it web sh
/ #

The container must be running: exec goes through its monitor. The command's output goes to exec only, not to the container's log. If exec goes away (the terminal closes), the command keeps running, as with Docker; when the container stops, every command started with exec stops with it, and a waiting exec exits 137. exec -d is not supported yet.

Exit codes: the command's own, or 125 when it could not be started: the container is not running or not found, the user is not in the image, or the command does not exist.

docs.title: ps
docs.text:
List containers: the running ones, or every one with -a. Newest first.

oci-hermit ps [-a] [-q] [--no-trunc]
Option Meaning -a, --all Include containers that are not running. -q, --quiet Only the IDs. --no-trunc Whole IDs and commands. 
$ oci-hermit ps -a
CONTAINER ID   IMAGE         COMMAND                  CREATED          STATUS                      PORTS   NAMES
1f0c2a9e4b7d   alpine:3.20   "sh -c 'sleep 60'"       10 seconds ago   Up 9 seconds                        job
8c3d5e0a1b2f   alpine:3.20   "cat /etc/alpine-rel…"   2 hours ago      Exited (0) 2 hours ago              quiet_nautilus

A container is running while its monitor is (see run). If the monitor was killed, the container shows as Exited (unknown); one that was killed shows Exited (137), and one that ended on stop's SIGTERM usually Exited (143) or the code its handler chose.

docs.title: logs
docs.text:
Show what a container's command printed, its stdout on stdout and its stderr on stderr, as it printed it.

oci-hermit logs [-f] <CONTAINER>
Option Meaning -f, --follow Keep showing new output until the container stops.

Every container keeps its output, whether it ran with -d or not, until it is removed. The log grows for as long as the container runs; there is no size limit yet.

$ oci-hermit logs -f ticker
Thu Nov 19 14:02:10 UTC 2026
Thu Nov 19 14:02:15 UTC 2026

docs.title: stop
docs.text:
Stop running containers. Prints each one as it was given, once it has stopped; exits 1 if any could not be stopped. A container that is not running is left as it is, and printed too.

oci-hermit stop [-t <SECONDS>] [-s <SIGNAL>] <CONTAINERS>...
Option Meaning -t, --time <SECONDS> How long to wait for the command to end before killing it. Default 10; 0 kills it at once. -s, --signal <SIGNAL> The signal to send first, instead of the image's StopSignal (SIGTERM when it has none).

As docker stop does: the container's command gets its stop signal, and if it is still running when the time is up, the sandbox is powered off and the container is recorded with exit code 137. Several containers stop at once. A command that handles SIGTERM (a web server, a shell script with trap … TERM) ends with its own exit code; one that ignores it, as PID 1 does without a handler, takes the full time.

$ oci-hermit stop -t 2 ticker
ticker

docs.title: kill
docs.text:
Send a signal to running containers' commands. Prints each one as it was given; exits 1 if any is not running or could not be signalled.

oci-hermit kill [-s <SIGNAL>] <CONTAINERS>...
Option Meaning -s, --signal <SIGNAL> The signal: a name such as TERM, SIGHUP or RTMIN+1, or a number. Default KILL.

The command decides what a signal does, except KILL, which always ends it (exit code 137). Signals go to the container's own command, not to commands started with exec.

$ oci-hermit kill -s HUP web
web

docs.title: rm
docs.text:
Remove containers that are not running, with their logs. Prints each one as it was given; exits 1 if any could not be removed.

oci-hermit rm [-f] <CONTAINERS>...

A container is named by its name, its ID, or the start of its ID. A running container is refused unless -f (--force) is given, which stops it first.

$ oci-hermit rm quiet_nautilus 1f0c
quiet_nautilus
oci-hermit: container job is running; stop it first (oci-hermit stop job), or remove it with rm -f
$ oci-hermit rm -f job
job

docs.title: pull
docs.text:
Pull an image from a registry into the store, for one platform, checking every digest.

oci-hermit pull [OPTIONS] <IMAGE>
Argument or option Meaning IMAGE An image reference, e.g. debian:bookworm-slim or ghcr.io/org/app:1.2. A digest (name@sha256:…) works too. --platform <PLATFORM> The platform to pull. Default: the host's. --cert-dir <DIR> Use the CA certificates (*.crt) and client certificate (*.cert with *.key) in DIR for this registry, instead of its certs.d folder. 
$ oci-hermit pull public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20
ab3fe4defd29: pulled (628 B)
3f26bc2dec0b: pulled (4.1 MB)
Digest: sha256:45e09956dc667c5eff3583c9d94830261fb1ca0be10a0a7db36266edf5de9e1d
Status: pulled public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20 for linux/arm64

Logins come from login and from the Podman and Docker auth files and credential helpers (see Pull from a private registry); with none, the pull is anonymous. Throttling and server errors are retried four times. A registry's own CA and client certificate come from its certs.d folder (see a registry with its own CA). Exits 0 on success, 1 on failure.

docs.title: manifest inspect
docs.text:
Show an image's index or manifest as the registry serves it, without pulling anything: which platforms it has, and each one's digest and size. Handy before a pull over a slow link, or to check that a private registry has the linux/amd64 or linux/arm64 build you need.

oci-hermit manifest inspect [OPTIONS] <IMAGE>
Argument or option Meaning IMAGE An image reference, as for pull; name@sha256:… works too. -v, --verbose Docker's verbose form: for each entry of an index, its descriptor (Descriptor) and the manifest it points to (OCIManifest, or SchemaV2Manifest for Docker's format), named by digest (Ref). For a single-platform image, the same for that manifest alone. --cert-dir <DIR> Use the CA certificates and client certificate in DIR for this registry, as for pull. 
$ oci-hermit manifest inspect ghcr.io/prefix-dev/pixi:0.84.2
{
  "manifests": [
    {
      "digest": "sha256:96b7c4d3efbd1d7b7ec8c6bb601545e8cf8ff62d6aedf4957cabc716e504cc50",
      "mediaType": "application/vnd.oci.image.manifest.v1+json",
      "platform": {
        "architecture": "amd64",
        "os": "linux"
      },
      "size": 1056
    },
    …

The JSON is the registry's, indented, with its keys in alphabetical order. Logins, certificates, plain-HTTP registries and retries work as for pull, and every manifest is checked against its digest. Nothing is stored. Exits 0 on success, 1 on failure.

docs.title: login
docs.text:
Log in to a registry. The user name and password are checked with the registry before anything is saved, as docker login does, then stored where Podman keeps logins, so pull, Podman and skopeo all use them.

oci-hermit login [OPTIONS] [REGISTRY]
Argument or option Meaning REGISTRY The registry's host name and port, e.g. ghcr.io or registry.example.com:5000. Default: docker.io. -u, --username <USERNAME> The user name. Asked for if not given. -p, --password <PASSWORD> The password or access token. Other users can see it in the process list, so it prints a warning; prefer --password-stdin. Asked for, without echo, if neither is given. --password-stdin Read the password from stdin. Needs --username. --authfile <AUTHFILE> Store the login in this file. Default: $REGISTRY_AUTH_FILE, else $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/containers/auth.json, else ~/.config/containers/auth.json. --get-login Print the user name logged in to REGISTRY, and nothing else. --cert-dir <DIR> Use the CA certificates and client certificate in DIR for this registry, as for pull. 
$ echo "$GHCR_TOKEN" | oci-hermit login -u your-user --password-stdin ghcr.io
Login Succeeded!

The file is written readable by you only (mode 0600 on Linux and macOS; on Windows it is in your user profile). A registry whose logins a credential helper keeps (credHelpers in that file) is refused. Exits 0 on success, 1 if the registry rejects the login, cannot be reached, or the options do not fit together; nothing is written then.

docs.title: logout
docs.text:
Remove a registry login from the file login writes.

oci-hermit logout [OPTIONS] [REGISTRY]
Argument or option Meaning REGISTRY The registry host. Default: docker.io. -a, --all Remove every login in the file. --authfile <AUTHFILE> Change this file instead. 
$ oci-hermit logout ghcr.io
Removed login credentials for ghcr.io

Exits 1 if there was no login to remove. A login made with docker login is in Docker's own file; logout names that file and suggests docker logout.

docs.title: load
docs.text:
Load images from an archive or a layout into the store, offline.

oci-hermit load --input <INPUT>
Option Meaning -i, --input <INPUT> A docker save or podman save archive (old or Docker 25+ format), an OCI archive (.tar), or an OCI layout directory.

Every platform in the archive is loaded, and every blob is checked against its digest. Each image keeps the name it was saved under; one without a name is stored under its image ID.

$ oci-hermit load -i alpine.tar
Loaded image: docker.io/mine/alpine:test (linux/arm64)
Loaded image: docker.io/mine/alpine:test (linux/amd64)
$ oci-hermit load -i ./unnamed
Loaded image ID: sha256:ab3fe4defd29ba6231229a4d41440ac8bde8218e85870e53876277faa24b35c4 (linux/arm64)

Exits 0 on success, 1 on failure. See Bring images in without a registry.

docs.title: images
docs.text:
List stored images, newest first, one row per name and platform. image ls and image list are the same command.

oci-hermit images [OPTIONS] [REFERENCE]
Argument or option Meaning REFERENCE Only images from this repository, or with this name. -q, --quiet Only show image IDs. --digests Show each image's manifest digest. --no-trunc Show full image IDs. 
$ oci-hermit images
REPOSITORY                             TAG             IMAGE ID       PLATFORM      CREATED        SIZE
public.ecr.aws/docker/library/debian   bookworm-slim   5b6c2c6cbc90   linux/arm64   12 days ago    28.1 MB
public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine   3.20            bf8527eb54c3   linux/amd64   7 months ago   3.6 MB
public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine   3.20            ab3fe4defd29   linux/arm64   7 months ago   4.1 MB

An image without a name shows <none> as its repository and tag.

docs.title: inspect
docs.text:
Show details of images as a JSON array, one object per name, close to podman image inspect. image inspect is the same command.

oci-hermit inspect <IMAGES>...

The fields are Id, Digest, RepoTags, RepoDigests, Created, Author, Architecture, Variant, Os, Size, Labels, Config, RootFS, History and ManifestType. An image that is not stored prints oci-hermit: no such image: <name> on stderr, and inspect exits 1. An example is in Manage the image store.

docs.title: tag
docs.text:
Give a stored image another name, for every platform stored under the source. Nothing is copied. image tag is the same command.

oci-hermit tag <SOURCE> <TARGET>

oci-hermit tag public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20 mine/alpine:test

docs.title: save
docs.text:
Save images to an archive that oci-hermit load, docker load, podman load and skopeo read. image save is the same command.

oci-hermit save [OPTIONS] --output <OUTPUT> <IMAGES>...
Argument or option Meaning IMAGES... Names or IDs. -o, --output <OUTPUT> The file to write. Required. --platform <PLATFORM> Only this platform, written in full (linux/arm64). Default: every platform stored.

The archive is an OCI image layout with a manifest.json beside it, the format Docker 25 and later write. See Move images between machines.

docs.title: rmi
docs.text:
Remove images by name or ID. Blobs no other image uses are deleted. image rm and image remove are the same command.

oci-hermit rmi [OPTIONS] <IMAGES>...
Option Meaning -f, --force Given an image ID with several names, remove every name. Without it, such an ID is refused. 
$ oci-hermit rmi public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20
Untagged: public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20
Deleted: sha256:bf8527eb54c3680e728d5b4b383a8ba730d72dae7236fbc8dff97ed6b224a731

Exits 1 if any name matched nothing or was refused. Refuses to run while another oci-hermit is using the store.

docs.title: image prune
docs.text:
Remove images loaded without a name, and every blob nothing uses.

oci-hermit image prune [OPTIONS]
Option Meaning -a, --all Remove every image, not only unnamed ones. -f, --force Do not ask for confirmation.

Without -f, it asks Are you sure you want to continue? [y/N] and goes ahead only on y or yes. Refuses to run while another oci-hermit is using the store.

docs.title: image history
docs.text:
Show the steps that built an image, newest first, with the size of the layer each made.

oci-hermit image history [OPTIONS] <IMAGE>
Option Meaning --no-trunc Do not shorten IDs and commands. -q, --quiet Only show image IDs.

docs.title: image exists
docs.text:
Exit 0 if an image is stored, 1 if not. Prints nothing.

oci-hermit image exists <IMAGE>

docs.title: system df
docs.text:
Show how much space the store uses. There are no containers yet, so every image counts as reclaimable.

$ oci-hermit system df
TYPE         TOTAL   ACTIVE   SIZE      RECLAIMABLE
Images       3       0        35.9 MB   35.9 MB (100%)
Containers   0       0        0 B       0 B

docs.title: machine info
docs.text:
Show the emulators, the guests, the defaults run uses, the image store and the registry auth files, and where each came from. oci-hermit info is the same command.

oci-hermit machine info

A full example is in Getting started, and every line is explained in Configuration. Exits 1 when the QEMU bundle is missing or is not the one oci-hermit was built for, because nothing can run then; a missing guest is shown but is not an error.

docs.title: machine boot
docs.text:
Boot a sandbox until its agent is ready, then stop it: a self-check of QEMU, the kernel and the agent. It needs no image.

oci-hermit machine boot [OPTIONS]
Option Meaning --arch <ARCH> Guest architecture: x86_64 or aarch64. Default: the host's. --memory <MEMORY> Memory for the sandbox, in MiB. Default 512. --cpus <CPUS> Number of emulated CPUs. Default 1. --timeout <TIMEOUT> Seconds to wait for the agent to be ready. Default 120. 
$ oci-hermit machine boot --arch x86_64
booting an x86_64 sandbox; console log: /var/folders/kb/…/T/oci-hermit/sandbox-12666-1794883275416245000/console.log
agent ready after 0.6s (control protocol 1.4)
guest powered off; sandbox stopped

Exits 0 when the guest booted and powered off, 1 otherwise; the error names the console and QEMU logs.

docs.title: version
docs.text:
Print the version and the control protocol version the host speaks.

$ oci-hermit version
oci-hermit 0.2.0 (control protocol 1.4)

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text: Code When 0 Success. 1 The command failed: a pull, load, image or container command (logs, stop, kill, rm) failed, image exists found nothing, machine info found no usable QEMU, machine boot did not boot. 2 The command is not implemented yet, or the command line is wrong (clap's usage errors). 125 run, exec: oci-hermit itself failed before or around the command. other run, exec: the command's own exit code.

docs.title: Planned commands
docs.text:
These are part of the command line already, so --help lists them, but they do nothing yet. Each prints oci-hermit:is not implemented yet; see …/ROADMAP.md and exits 2:

Not in the command line yet, and planned:
