docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: oci-hermit has no configuration file. It finds what it needs beside itself, keeps images in your data folder, and reads a few environment variables. oci-hermit machine info shows the result.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
Variable What it does Default OCI_HERMIT_DATA_DIR Where the image store (images/) and the containers (containers/) live. The platform's per-user data folder: see Where things are kept. OCI_HERMIT_QEMU_DIR A QEMU bundle to use, a folder with bin/qemu-system-x86_64 and bin/qemu-system-aarch64. Searched first. qemu/ beside oci-hermit, or <prefix>/libexec/oci-hermit/qemu for a prefix install. OCI_HERMIT_GUEST_DIR A guest to use, a folder with kernel, hermit-agent and crun in x86_64/ and aarch64/. Searched first. guest/ beside oci-hermit, or <prefix>/libexec/oci-hermit/guest. OCI_HERMIT_INSECURE_REGISTRIES Registries to reach over plain HTTP, as host:port, comma separated. None: every registry needs HTTPS. OCI_HERMIT_TIMINGS Anything but empty or 0 makes run print how long each phase took, on stderr. Off. REGISTRY_AUTH_FILE An auth file to read first, as Podman does. Not set. XDG_RUNTIME_DIR Podman's runtime auth file is $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/containers/auth.json. Set by the system on most Linux desktops. XDG_CONFIG_HOME Podman's auth file is $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/containers/auth.json. ~/.config DOCKER_CONFIG Docker's auth file is $DOCKER_CONFIG/config.json. ~/.docker XDG_DATA_HOME Linux only: the image store is $XDG_DATA_HOME/oci-hermit. ~/.local/share HOME, USERPROFILE, LOCALAPPDATA Where the defaults above start. USERPROFILE stands in for HOME on Windows. Set by the system. TMPDIR (TMP on Windows) Where each sandbox's folder goes, in oci-hermit/. The system's temp folder. TERM Passed to a command run with -t, unless the image sets its own. xterm PATH Where credential helpers (docker-credential-*) are found.

An empty value counts as not set.

Set a variable for one command or for the session:

macOS and LinuxWindows 
OCI_HERMIT_DATA_DIR=/tmp/scratch-store oci-hermit images     # one command
export OCI_HERMIT_DATA_DIR=/tmp/scratch-store                # this session

$env:OCI_HERMIT_DATA_DIR = "$env:TEMP\scratch-store"         # this session
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("OCI_HERMIT_DATA_DIR", "D:\oci-hermit", "User")   # for good, new windows

docs.title: Where things are kept
docs.text:
What Windows macOS Linux Image store %LOCALAPPDATA%\oci-hermit\images ~/Library/Application Support/oci-hermit/images $XDG_DATA_HOME/oci-hermit/images, or ~/.local/share/oci-hermit/images Containers %LOCALAPPDATA%\oci-hermit\containers ~/Library/Application Support/oci-hermit/containers $XDG_DATA_HOME/oci-hermit/containers, or ~/.local/share/oci-hermit/containers Containers' control sockets named pipes, \\.\pipe\oci-hermit-<id> ~/Library/Application Support/oci-hermit/sockets $XDG_DATA_HOME/oci-hermit/sockets, or ~/.local/share/oci-hermit/sockets Each sandbox's initramfs and logs %TMP%\oci-hermit\sandbox-* $TMPDIR/oci-hermit/sandbox-* $TMPDIR/oci-hermit/sandbox-*, or /tmp/oci-hermit/sandbox-* QEMU, kernel and agent the qemu/ and guest/ folders beside oci-hermit the same the same A registry's own CAs and client certificate ~\.config\containers\certs.d\<host><port>\, or Docker's ~/.config/containers/certs.d/<host:port>/, or /etc/containers/certs.d, or Docker's the same as macOS

Each container is a folder named by its ID in containers/: container.json (what it runs, from which image, its name), state.json (running or exited, its exit code), container.log (its output, for logs) and launch.json (how its monitor starts the sandbox). oci-hermit rm removes it; run --rm removes it when the command ends.

A running container's monitor listens for stop on a Unix socket in sockets/, a folder only you can open, or on Windows on a named pipe that refuses other machines. A socket's path must fit in 103 bytes, so on Linux and macOS OCI_HERMIT_DATA_DIR cannot be a very deep folder: run says so if it is.

oci-hermit never writes beside itself, so its folder can be read-only. It does not delete old sandbox-* folders: each holds the initramfs (about the image's size) and the logs of one run or machine boot (console.log, qemu.log, and for a run the monitor's monitor.log). Delete them when you no longer need the logs.

The image store is an OCI image layout: index.json names the images, blobs/sha256/ holds their contents, and lock and index.lock coordinate several oci-hermit processes. Change it only through oci-hermit's commands.

Each sandbox folder holds:

File What it is initrd.cpio The initramfs the guest boots: the agent as /init, and for run the image's files under /rootfs. console.log The guest's serial console: the kernel's boot messages and the agent's hermit-agent: … lines. qemu.log QEMU's own messages (its stderr).

docs.title: How oci-hermit finds QEMU and the guest
docs.text:
For each, the first folder that has everything wins:

  1. the folder named by OCI_HERMIT_QEMU_DIR (or OCI_HERMIT_GUEST_DIR);
  2. <prefix>/libexec/oci-hermit/qemu (or …/guest), when oci-hermit is installed as <prefix>/bin/oci-hermit, as a conda or pixi global package will be;
  3. qemu/ (or guest/) beside the oci-hermit executable, as in the downloaded package.

A QEMU found this way must be the bundle oci-hermit was built for: --version must report 11.1.3 (oci-hermit-qemu-4) and offer the tcg accelerator, and the x86_64 firmware must be there. Any other QEMU, even the same release from elsewhere, is refused. A missing guest for one architecture only stops images of that architecture.

docs.title: What machine info shows
docs.text:
$ oci-hermit machine info
oci-hermit 0.2.0 (control protocol 1.4)
host: macos/aarch64, so images default to linux/arm64

The version, and the host's OS and architecture, which decide the default image platform.

emulator (QEMU, software CPU only):
  bundle:     /Users/me/oci-hermit/qemu (found beside oci-hermit)
  x86_64:     QEMU 11.1.3 (oci-hermit-qemu-4), accel tcg
  aarch64:    QEMU 11.1.3 (oci-hermit-qemu-4), accel tcg

The QEMU bundle, and where it was found: from OCI_HERMIT_QEMU_DIR or found beside oci-hermit. Each emulator's version and accelerator. A problem here makes machine info exit 1, with the reason on stderr.

guest (kernel and agent each sandbox boots):
  x86_64:     /Users/me/oci-hermit/guest/x86_64 (kernel 2.9 MB, agent 1.3 MB, found beside oci-hermit)
  aarch64:    /Users/me/oci-hermit/guest/aarch64 (kernel 5.9 MB, agent 1.2 MB, found beside oci-hermit)

Each guest, its sizes and where it was found. A missing one says not found; <platform> images cannot run.

sandbox defaults for run:
  cpus:       1 (--cpus)
  memory:     512 MiB for a stored image (its layers are disks); twice the size of one run from a file, plus 256 MiB (--memory)
  network:    none: no egress; -p (127.0.0.1 only) is not implemented yet
  run dir:    /var/folders/kb/…/T/oci-hermit (a sandbox-* folder per run: initramfs, console.log, qemu.log)

What run gives a sandbox unless told otherwise, and where the sandbox folders go.

image store (pull, load):
  path:       /Users/me/Library/Application Support/oci-hermit/images (the platform default)
  images:     3 images under 2 names (one per name and platform)
  size:       35.9 MB

The store, whether its path is the platform default or from OCI_HERMIT_DATA_DIR, and what it holds.

registries (pulls happen on the host, never in the sandbox):
  auth files: searched in this order; the first with a login for the registry is used
    1. [not set]   $REGISTRY_AUTH_FILE
    2. [not set]   $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/containers/auth.json
    3. [not found] /Users/me/.config/containers/auth.json
    4. [found]     /Users/me/.docker/config.json
  plain http: none (OCI_HERMIT_INSECURE_REGISTRIES)

Every auth file, in the order they are read: [not set] when the variable it needs is not set, [not found] when the file does not exist, [found] when it does. Then the registries reached over plain HTTP. See Pull from a private registry.

docs.title: oci-hermit — Design
docs.text: Status: draft, 2026-11-15

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Build a single-binary tool that runs prebuilt OCI images inside a software-emulated Linux sandbox on Linux, Windows and macOS. It needs no root, no admin rights, no hardware virtualization and no WSL. Each sandbox is a small emulated VM: images are unpacked on the host without privileges, handed to the guest as read-only disks, and started by crun inside the guest. Networking is sealed: no egress, and ingress only through ports the user publishes on the host's 127.0.0.1.

Goals

  • Test prebuilt container images on locked-down laptops where Docker, Podman machines and WSL are unavailable.
  • Strong isolation: the guest never runs directly on the host CPU and has no route out.
  • A Docker/Podman-style CLI, including a Compose subset for frontend-plus-backend apps.
  • One portable codebase, written in Rust.

Non-goals

  • Building images. npm install, pixi install and similar run before the image reaches this tool.
  • Native-speed or production workloads.
  • Bridge or host networking, privileged containers, device passthrough.

docs.title: Requirements and constraints
docs.text: Requirement Decision Host platforms Linux, Windows, macOS (x86-64 and arm64 hosts) Privileges None: no root, no admin, no installer drivers Hardware virtualization Not required; pure software CPU emulation WSL Not used Egress Blocked, always Ingress Only explicitly published ports, bound to 127.0.0.1 In-sandbox networking Loopback works; containers in one pod share localhost Images Prebuilt OCI images: registry pull, OCI layout or tarball Workloads Smoke-testing images: web frontends and backends, interactive shells Host folders Bind mounts allowed, read-only by default CLI Mirrors Docker and Podman commands

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Each sandbox is one emulator process that the host tool launches as the user. Every path into the guest passes through a host-tool component and a single virtio device, and there is no path out.

flowchart TB
    subgraph inputs[Host inputs]
        term[Terminal<br/>run, exec, compose]
        browser[Host browser<br/>127.0.0.1:8080]
        folders[Host folders<br/>ro by default]
        registry[OCI registry<br/>or local tarball]
    end

    subgraph host[Host tool — Rust, runs as you, no admin]
        cli[CLI and state]
        ports[Port publisher<br/>binds 127.0.0.1 only]
        ninep[9P file server<br/>enforces mount policy]
        store[Image store<br/>EROFS layer cache]
    end

    subgraph qemu[QEMU, software CPU — TCG: the security boundary]
        ctl[Control channel<br/>virtio-serial]
        nic[Restricted NIC<br/>slirp, restrict=on]
        fch[File channel<br/>virtio-serial, 9P]
        disks[Layer disks<br/>virtio-blk, read-only]

        subgraph guest[Guest Linux VM — minimal kernel]
            agent[Guest agent, PID 1<br/>mounts layers and 9P<br/>starts containers via crun<br/>relays published ports]
            subgraph pod[Pod: containers share localhost]
                fe[Frontend container]
                be[Backend container]
            end
            rootfs[Container root: read-only layers + throwaway writable layer]
        end
    end

    internet[(Internet and LAN)]

    term --> cli
    browser --> ports
    folders --> ninep
    registry --> store
    cli --> ctl
    ports --> nic
    ninep --> fch
    store --> disks
    ctl --> agent
    nic --> pod
    fch --> agent
    disks --> rootfs
    guest -. blocked: no route out .-x internet

Read it top to bottom: inputs reach the host tool, each host-tool component speaks to the guest through one device, and the guest agent wires those devices into the pod. The QEMU process is the security boundary.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
Host tool (Rust, single binary). Owns everything on the host side and is the only process the user runs.

  • CLI front end and a small state store (images, containers, pods) under the user's data directory.
  • Image store: pulls and verifies images from registries, or loads OCI layouts and tarballs offline.
  • Layer builder: turns each layer into a read-only EROFS disk image, cached by digest.
  • Sandbox supervisor: launches and monitors one emulator process per sandbox, applies CPU and memory limits. QEMU is started with -accel tcg -nodefaults -no-user-config -display none -no-reboot, the console on a log file, and no network yet. It exits with the host tool: -run-with exit-with-parent=on on Linux and macOS, a kill-on-close Job Object on Windows. oci-hermit machine boot boots one sandbox until the agent is ready, as a self-check.
  • Container monitor (#22): each container's sandbox belongs to a background oci-hermit __monitor process of its own, like Podman's conmon, with no daemon. It holds the container's running lock, owns QEMU, writes the output to the container's log and records the exit code. Other commands reach it over an owner-only local channel (a Unix socket in the data folder; a named pipe on Windows): run attaches to it, stop asks it to stop, exec asks it to start another command in the container (protocol 1.5, crun exec in the guest). A foreground run that goes away takes its container with it; run -d leaves it running.
  • Control client: talks to the guest agent over the virtio-serial port org.oci-hermit.control. QEMU wires that port to its own stdin and stdout, which the host tool holds as an anonymous pipe pair, so nothing on the filesystem or network can reach it. Messages are newline-delimited JSON (hermit-proto), at most 64 KiB a line; a session opens with Hello/Ready (major versions must match) and ends with Shutdown/ShuttingDown. Anything else from either side gets an error reply, and the host never trusts the guest to behave.
  • 9P file server: serves bind-mounted folders and enforces the mount policy.
  • Port publisher: listens on 127.0.0.1 and relays connections into the guest.

Emulator (bundled QEMU, TCG mode). A helper process launched by the host tool. oci-hermit builds it itself, TCG-only, and refuses any other QEMU (qemu/README.md).

  • microvm machine type for x86_64 guests and virt for aarch64 ones, virtio devices only: block disks, one network card, serial channels, console.
  • Multi-threaded TCG so a sandbox can have several vCPUs.
  • Emulates x86-64 or arm64 guests on any host, so --platform works everywhere.

Guest kernel. A minimal Linux kernel built by the project: virtio, overlayfs, EROFS, 9P, namespaces and cgroups. Nothing else. It is the newest LTS release, configured from tinyconfig plus committed fragments; see guest/README.md.

Guest agent (Rust, static, PID 1).

  • Boots as init: mounts /proc, /sys, devtmpfs on /dev, devpts, and tmpfs on /run and /tmp (an already-mounted target is skipped), logs line-oriented hermit-agent: ... messages to the console, and reaps orphaned children.
  • Never exits: on a shutdown request or any fatal setup error it logs, syncs and powers the VM off, because a PID 1 that exits or panics panics the kernel. The shutdown request is the host's Shutdown message, or SIGTERM or SIGINT; the agent logs a ready line with the protocol version once it is waiting. Run anywhere other than as PID 1 on Linux, it refuses to start.
  • A static binary per guest architecture (pixi run -e agent agent-build, x86-64 and arm64). It is static glibc (crt-static, conda-forge's 2.39 sysroot) rather than musl, because conda-forge ships no musl Rust standard library.
  • Mounts the layer disks and builds an overlayfs root with a throwaway writable layer.
  • Mounts bind-mounted folders over 9P.
  • Generates OCI runtime bundles and starts containers with crun.
  • Handles exec, PTYs, logs, signals and exit codes for the host tool.
  • Runs containers of one pod in a shared network namespace.

run today. A stored image runs through the image pipeline below. An image opened from a path (an OCI layout directory or .tar), or one with more layers than a sandbox takes disks, is applied in memory instead and its files go into the initramfs under /rootfs. Either way the agent writes an OCI runtime bundle (/run/oci-hermit/config.json, with Docker's default namespaces, capabilities, masked paths and device rules) and starts the command with crun run, on a pty crun hands over through a console socket for -t or on pipes otherwise, then relays it over the control channel and reports its exit code. crun's pivot_root refuses an initramfs root, so at boot the agent moves its root onto a tmpfs, as switch_root does. Seccomp (#102) is not applied yet.

Image pipeline. pull or load → verify digests → per-layer EROFS image (cached) → attached read-only to the VM → stacked with overlayfs in the guest. The host never mounts anything, so no privileges are needed.

docs.title: Networking
docs.text:
The sandbox has no egress at all. The only way in is a port the user publishes, and it is bound to the host's 127.0.0.1.

  • Starting point: QEMU user-mode networking (libslirp) with restrict=on. The guest cannot reach the host or anything beyond it, and explicit forwarding rules still work. -p 8080:80 becomes a forward from 127.0.0.1:8080 on the host to port 80 in the guest.
  • Inside the sandbox: loopback works normally. Containers in one pod share a network namespace, so a frontend reaches its backend on localhost.
  • Binding rule: published ports bind to 127.0.0.1 even when the user asks for 0.0.0.0. Exposing to the LAN would need an explicit opt-in flag, not in the first release.
  • Stronger later option: remove the guest NIC entirely. The guest agent accepts relayed connections over virtio-serial and connects to the container's port on loopback. With no network device, there is no network stack exposed to the guest.
  • Image pulls happen in the host tool only. The guest never sees registry credentials or a route out.
  • Failure is a feature: an image that tries to download things at runtime fails, which proves it isn't self-contained.

docs.title: Filesystem and bind mounts
docs.text:
The container root is an overlay of read-only image layers plus a throwaway writable layer, discarded when the container is removed. Host folders can be bind-mounted, read-only unless the user says otherwise.

Mechanism. The host tool runs its own 9P server and carries it over a virtio-serial channel. The guest agent mounts it with the Linux 9P client in trans=fd mode, then bind-mounts it into the container. The same code works on all three host OSes, and every file operation passes through code the project controls.

Mount policy, enforced by the 9P server:

  • Read-only by default. -v ./src:/app is read-only; writing needs :rw. This is a deliberate difference from Docker.
  • No escaping the shared root: .., outward symlinks and Windows junctions are refused. On Linux, openat2 with RESOLVE_BENEATH does this in the kernel.
  • Deny-list of sources: drive roots, the whole home folder, ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, ~/.kube, ~/.docker and OS credential stores.
  • No device nodes, FIFOs or sockets. Setuid bits and host ownership are ignored; files appear owned by the container user.
  • Every active mount and its mode is shown in oci-hermit inspect and oci-hermit ps.

Syntax follows Docker: -v src:dst[:ro|:rw] and --mount type=bind,src=,dst=,readonly. Compose volumes: entries follow the same rules. Named volumes come later.

Documented trade-off: an :rw mount is an intentional hole. Anything the container writes there lands on the host.

docs.title: CLI and Compose subset
docs.text:
Commands mirror Docker and Podman so existing habits carry over. oci-hermit is the binary name. A short name, hrmt, ships beside it for daily use (#44). No bare hermit binary is shipped, to avoid clashing with Cash App's Hermit on a user's PATH.

# Images (host side)
oci-hermit pull ghcr.io/org/app:1.2
oci-hermit load -i app.tar            # docker-archive or OCI layout
oci-hermit images | rmi | inspect | tag | save | image prune | image history | image exists
oci-hermit system df

# Containers
oci-hermit run -it --rm alpine sh
oci-hermit run -d --name web -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 -v ./data:/data app:1.2
oci-hermit exec -it web sh
oci-hermit logs -f web
oci-hermit ps -a | stop | rm | cp

# Pods (shared localhost, like podman pod)
oci-hermit pod create --name shop -p 8080:3000
oci-hermit run -d --pod shop backend:1.0
oci-hermit run -d --pod shop frontend:1.0

# Compose subset
oci-hermit compose up -d
oci-hermit compose down

# Sandbox details
oci-hermit machine info
oci-hermit machine boot [--arch x86_64|aarch64]   # boot a sandbox until its agent is ready

Deliberate differences from Docker

Area Behaviour -p Always binds to 127.0.0.1 --network Only none and pod-shared; no bridge or host Refused flags --privileged, --cap-add, --device, host PID or IPC namespaces -v Read-only unless :rw --cpus, --memory Size the emulated VM Compose services, image, ports, environment, command, depends_on, healthcheck, volumes; build: rejected

A Compose project runs as one pod in one sandbox VM.

docs.title: Security model
docs.text:
The security boundary is the emulator process: guest code never runs directly on the host CPU, and it can only touch the devices the emulator provides. Defence in depth comes from keeping that boundary small and locking down the process around it.

Layers, outermost first

  1. Host OS sandbox around the emulator, using unprivileged features: seccomp and Landlock on Linux, App Sandbox on macOS, an AppContainer or low-integrity token on Windows.
  2. Software CPU emulation (TCG). No hypervisor or kernel driver on the host.
  3. Minimal device model: virtio block, serial and (initially) one restricted NIC. No USB, graphics, sound or shared clipboard.
  4. Guest kernel separating the container from the agent.
  5. Container namespaces and cgroups inside the guest, via crun.

What the guest can reach: its own read-only layer disks, its writable layer, published-port connections coming in, and bind-mounted folders under the mount policy. Nothing else.

Host-side code is Rust, removing most memory-safety bugs from the parts that parse guest input (9P, control protocol, port relay).

Supply chain: image digests are verified on pull. Signature verification (cosign or notation) is a later milestone. Release binaries are code-signed on Windows and macOS.

docs.title: Performance expectations
docs.text:
Software emulation is slower than native, but the target workloads are light because images arrive fully built.

Activity Expectation Sandbox start About 1 to 1.5 seconds on a recent laptop, 2 to 6 on CI runners; see Measured start times Interactive shell Responsive Web frontend and backend under test traffic Acceptable for smoke tests CPU-heavy work (compiles, large data loads) Several times to more than 10x slower than native; out of scope

Levers if needed: layer caching, a pre-booted kernel snapshot, and more vCPUs through multi-threaded TCG.

docs.title: Measured start times
docs.text:
Time from oci-hermit run to a shell in the Debian 12 slim image, then back out: oci-hermit run debian.tar bash -ic exit, release build, one vCPU; each row is the run with the median total out of three. Set OCI_HERMIT_TIMINGS=1 to have run print the same breakdown on stderr:

  • Prepare: read the image, apply its layers and write the initramfs.
  • Boot: start QEMU, boot the kernel and wait for the agent to say it is ready.
  • Command: start the command and wait for it to exit (here, an interactive bash that exits at once).
  • Stop: power the guest off.
Host Guest Prepare Boot Command Stop Total Apple M4 Mac, macOS 26.2 aarch64 0.31s 0.58s 0.05s 0.02s 0.96s Apple M4 Mac, macOS 26.2 x86_64 0.29s 1.09s 0.05s 0.03s 1.45s GitHub ubuntu-24.04-arm (Linux arm64) aarch64 0.37s 1.40s 0.09s 0.02s 1.88s GitHub ubuntu-24.04-arm (Linux arm64) x86_64 0.34s 3.75s 0.11s 0.02s 4.22s GitHub ubuntu-latest (Ubuntu 26.04, x64) aarch64 0.49s 1.46s 0.11s 0.02s 2.08s GitHub ubuntu-latest (Ubuntu 26.04, x64) x86_64 0.41s 2.41s 0.13s 0.02s 2.98s GitHub windows-latest (Windows Server 2025, x64) aarch64 0.70s 1.43s 0.11s 0.02s 2.26s GitHub windows-latest (Windows Server 2025, x64) x86_64 0.52s 2.80s 0.16s 0.04s 3.54s GitHub macos-latest (macOS 26, Apple silicon) aarch64 0.49s 2.35s 0.12s 0.09s 3.04s GitHub macos-latest (macOS 26, Apple silicon) x86_64 0.50s 2.93s 0.14s 0.03s 3.61s GitHub macos-15-intel (macOS 15, Intel) aarch64 0.96s 4.91s 0.24s 0.06s 6.17s GitHub macos-15-intel (macOS 15, Intel) x86_64 0.61s 3.32s 0.19s 0.04s 4.17s

The CI rows come from the hosts job in kernel.yml, which records the same three runs in every job summary. Hosted runners are small shared VMs (3 or 4 vCPUs), so they are slower and noisier than a laptop; the Intel macOS runner varied most, from 5.3s to 7.4s for the aarch64 guest.

Boot dominates everywhere, and a sandbox is ready in 1 to 6 seconds. An x86_64 guest boots more slowly than an aarch64 one on every host except the Intel Mac, where the order flips. These runs are from a file, so the image is copied into the initramfs and prepare grows with its size; a stored image runs from its EROFS layer disks (#16, #17) instead.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
No existing tool combines rootless, no-hypervisor, cross-platform and a Docker-style UX.

Project What it does Gap for this use container2wasm Converts an image to Wasm that runs Linux and the container on an emulated CPU Experimental; per-image conversion; no Docker-style CLI Blink Unprivileged user-space emulator for x86-64 Linux binaries Forwards syscalls to the host, so no sandbox; Windows only via Cygwin without JIT VirtualBox Full VMs Software virtualization removed in 6.1; needs VT-x or Hyper-V and admin-installed drivers Podman rootless Native rootless containers Linux only; needs a VM on Windows and macOS Lima, Podman machine, Docker Desktop Linux VM for containers Need a hypervisor; some need admin or WSL

docs.title: Packaging, risks and open questions
docs.text:
Packaging decision: a standalone tool, published on conda-forge so pixi global install, pixi add and conda install all work. It is not a pixi extension, because its audience is anyone testing images and it ships its own emulator, kernel and agent. A thin pixi-oci-hermit shim or a pixi-oci hook can add a build-then-smoke-test flow later.

Risks

Risk Mitigation Endpoint allow-listing (AppLocker, Defender) blocks an unsigned emulator on corporate laptops Code-signed releases on Windows and macOS from the first release QEMU is GPL-2.0 Ship it as a separate helper process, not linked into the host tool; publish its source 9P over virtio-serial is too slow for large bind mounts Prototype early; fall back to QEMU's built-in 9P where it works Emulation too slow for some test suites Scope to smoke tests; document limits; measure in milestone 1 Guest-to-emulator escape bugs OS sandbox around the emulator; minimal device model; track QEMU security fixes

Open questions

  • conda-forge has no system-emulation QEMU for macOS or Windows, so oci-hermit builds its own minimal one (qemu/README.md).
  • Keep libslirp long-term, or move to the NIC-less relay design?
  • Project name: oci-hermit (free on conda-forge, crates.io, PyPI, npm and GitHub as of 2026-11-15).
  • Signature verification: cosign, notation, or both?

docs.title: Milestones
docs.text: See ROADMAP.md.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
Everything runs through pixi, which provides the Rust toolchain and every other tool from conda-forge. Clone the repository and install the hooks once:

git clone https://github.com/millsks/oci-hermit
cd oci-hermit
pixi run bootstrap        # pre-commit and commit-msg hooks

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
Task What it runs pixi run fmt cargo fmt --all pixi run lint clippy on the whole workspace, warnings as errors pixi run check cargo check on the whole workspace pixi run test cargo test --workspace; one test: pixi run cargo test -p oci-hermit <name> pixi run build a release build of the workspace pixi run cov the tests under cargo llvm-cov, failing below 90% line coverage pixi run ci the full gate: pre-commit, build, check, clippy, coverage pixi run -e lint deny cargo deny: advisories, licences, banned crates and sources pixi run -e msrv msrv-check cargo check on the oldest supported Rust pixi run -e agent agent-build the static guest agent (Linux only) pixi run -e qemu-build qemu-build the QEMU bundle into qemu/out (Linux and macOS) pixi run -e kernel-build kernel-build [arch] [out-dir] the guest kernel (Linux only, natively per architecture) pixi run -e docs docs-serve this site, served locally with live reload pixi run -e docs docs-build this site, built strictly into site/

The pre-commit hooks run rustfmt, clippy, taplo (TOML), typos, actionlint (workflows) and the usual file checks; the commit-msg hook enforces Conventional Commits.

docs.title: Running a source build
docs.text:
A source build needs a QEMU bundle and a guest. Take them from the package in Getting started, or from CI artifacts, and point the build at them:

pixi run cargo build --release -p oci-hermit
export OCI_HERMIT_QEMU_DIR=/path/to/oci-hermit/qemu
export OCI_HERMIT_GUEST_DIR=/path/to/oci-hermit/guest
target/release/oci-hermit machine boot

Keep test images out of your real store with OCI_HERMIT_DATA_DIR:

export OCI_HERMIT_DATA_DIR=$(mktemp -d)

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
• Work on a branch and open a pull request against main; link the issue it resolves.
  • Commit messages follow Conventional Commits (feat(run): …, fix(load): …, docs: …).
  • Every change comes with tests, and pixi run ci passes before you push.
  • The CI result check is the one a pull request needs.

docs.title: Continuous integration
docs.text: Workflow What it does ci.yml pre-commit, fmt, clippy and check; tests on Linux x64 and arm64, macOS and Windows; the coverage gate; cargo deny; the MSRV; the static agent for both architectures. CI result sums them up. qemu.yml Builds the QEMU bundle for all five hosts and checks each with machine info. kernel.yml Builds and boot-tests both kernels, builds the agent, then on every kind of host boots both guests, runs a Debian image (output, exit code, stdin, a terminal), pulls and loads images, measures start times, runs as a standard user without admin rights, and packages the per-host folders that Getting started downloads. docs.yml Builds this site strictly on pull requests that touch it; publishes it to GitHub Pages from main (dev) and from releases.

docs.title: The documentation site
docs.text:
The site is MkDocs with the Material theme, set up as pixi-sbom's is. Pages live in docs/; mkdocs.yml holds the navigation. A few repository files are published as pages without copies in docs/ (SECURITY.md, ROADMAP.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, CHANGELOG.md, qemu/README.md, guest/README.md): mkdocs_hooks.py adds them, and points links that leave docs/ at the page that publishes their target, or at the file on GitHub. Write links as they work on GitHub (../ROADMAP.md); the hook takes care of the site.

pixi run -e docs docs-serve     # http://127.0.0.1:8000
pixi run -e docs docs-build     # fails on any broken link or anchor

Versions are published with mike: dev follows main, each release gets its own copy, and latest is the newest release.

docs.title: Design discussions
docs.text: Changes to the design start in an issue. The design document is the reference, and the roadmap says what comes when.

docs.title: oci-hermit, Docker and Podman
docs.text: oci-hermit takes Docker's and Podman's commands, so habits carry over: pull, load, images, run -it, rmi and the rest mean what you expect. It reads the same images, the same archives and the same registry logins. Some things differ on purpose, because the point of oci-hermit is a sandbox that needs nothing from the machine and lets nothing out.

docs.title: How it runs
docs.text: Docker and Podman oci-hermit Privileges Docker needs a daemon running as root, or rootless set-up by an admin. Podman is rootless on Linux. None. A folder you unpack and run as yourself. Virtualization On Windows and macOS, a Linux VM under a hypervisor (WSL 2, Hyper-V, Apple's Virtualization framework). A VM with an emulated CPU (QEMU TCG). Nothing to enable. Daemon Docker has a daemon; Podman machine has a VM that stays up. Neither. Each run boots its own VM and powers it off when the command ends. Kernel The host's (Linux) or the VM's. oci-hermit's own minimal Linux 6.18 kernel, the same on every host. Runtime runc or crun, with namespaces and cgroups. crun inside the VM, with Docker's default namespaces, capabilities, masked paths and devices; no seccomp profile yet (#102). The VM is the main boundary. Speed Native, or close to it. Emulated: roughly 5 to 20 times slower for CPU work. See Performance and limits. Other architectures Through QEMU user-mode emulation (binfmt), set up separately. Built in: amd64 and arm64 images run on every host.

docs.title: Deliberate differences
docs.text:
Area Docker and Podman oci-hermit Outbound network The container can reach the network. Never. The sandbox has no network device. There is no flag to turn it on. Published ports (-p, planned in #27) Bind to all interfaces (0.0.0.0) unless you name one. Always bind to 127.0.0.1, even if you ask for 0.0.0.0. Bind mounts (-v, planned in #33) Read-write unless you add :ro. Read-only unless you add :rw. Sensitive folders (~/.ssh, ~/.aws, ~/.kube, ~/.docker, the whole home folder, drive roots) are refused. --network (planned) bridge, host, user networks. Only none and a pod's shared network. --privileged, --cap-add, --device, --pid host, --ipc host (planned) Accepted. Refused. --cpus, --memory Limits for the container. The size of the emulated VM. stop The stop signal (SIGTERM), then SIGKILL after 10 seconds. The same; the kill is powering the sandbox off, exit code 137. kill, Ctrl-C kill sends any signal; run passes on the signals it gets. The same, to the container's command only (not to exec's, as with Docker). Running containers Kept by a daemon (dockerd) or, in Podman, by a conmon process per container. Kept by a monitor process per container, as Podman's conmon; no daemon. A run without -d takes its container down with it if it is killed. exec -u <name> Looks the name up in the container's current /etc/passwd. Looks it up in the image's: a user added inside the running container needs its number. exec -d is not supported yet. Containers Kept after they stop, until rm, with their files. Kept after they stop, until rm (--rm removes them at once), but only as a record and the output: name, image, command, exit code and logs. The files a command changed go with its sandbox. Building images build Not supported; build elsewhere (#50 discusses it). Compose (planned in #36, #37) Full Compose. A subset: services, image, ports, environment, command, depends_on, healthcheck, volumes. build: is refused.

A flag that exists but is not implemented yet is refused with its issue number, never ignored. See the command-line reference for what is planned.

docs.title: What is shared with them
docs.text:
• Images and names. The same references, with Docker's expansion: alpine is docker.io/library/alpine:latest.
  • Registry logins. oci-hermit login and logout work as podman login and podman logout do and write the same file; oci-hermit also reads Docker's auth file and runs Docker credential helpers (Pull from a private registry).
  • Archives. oci-hermit load reads docker save and podman save archives; oci-hermit save writes the Docker 25 format, which docker load and podman load read.
  • Exit codes. run exits with the command's code, or 125 when oci-hermit itself fails, as docker run does.

oci-hermit never talks to a Docker daemon or to Podman, and does not share their image stores: an image you pulled with Docker is not visible to oci-hermit until you docker save it and oci-hermit load it.

docs.title: When to use which
docs.text:
Use Docker or Podman where you can: for building images, for anything that needs the network, for performance, and for the final check before you deploy. Use oci-hermit where they are not an option, such as a locked-down laptop, or when you want a sealed sandbox that cannot reach anything. When to use oci-hermit goes into more detail.

If Docker and Podman are blocked on your machine on purpose, check that running an emulator is allowed before you use oci-hermit there. Needing no admin rights is not the same as being permitted.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This page takes you from nothing to a shell in a Linux image on Windows, macOS or Linux. None of it needs admin rights, a hypervisor or WSL. Pick your operating system in any of the tabs below; the others follow.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
One file per kind of machine, from the releases page. Each unpacks into one folder that runs from wherever you put it:

oci-hermit/
  oci-hermit(.exe)        the host tool
  hrmt(.exe)              the same program under a shorter name
  qemu/                   the bundled emulator (QEMU, TCG only)
  guest/x86_64/           the guest kernel and agent, for x86_64 (amd64) images
  guest/aarch64/          the same for arm64 images
  LICENSE                 oci-hermit's license (Apache-2.0)
  THIRD-PARTY-LICENSES    every bundled component and its license
  README.txt

oci-hermit finds qemu/ and guest/ next to itself, so there is nothing to configure. Both guests run on every host, because the CPU is emulated: an arm64 image runs on an Intel PC, and an amd64 image runs on a Mac with Apple silicon.

Your machine File Windows, x64 oci-hermit-<version>-win-64.zip macOS, Apple silicon oci-hermit-<version>-osx-arm64.tar.gz macOS, Intel oci-hermit-<version>-osx-64.tar.gz Linux, x86-64 oci-hermit-<version>-linux-64.tar.gz Linux, arm64 oci-hermit-<version>-linux-aarch64.tar.gz

Each release starts as a pre-release. Once it has been tried on a managed Windows machine on a private network, it becomes the Latest release; take that one unless you want to try the newest. The binaries are not signed yet (#39), so Windows and macOS warn the first time; see If it will not start.

docs.title: 1. Download
docs.text:
With a browser: open the releases page, and under Assets of the newest release download the file for your machine. No GitHub account is needed. Unpack it: on Windows, right-click the .zip and choose Extract All; on macOS, double-click the .tar.gz.

From a terminal, with the GitHub CLI (gh):

WindowsmacOSLinux

In PowerShell:

$tag = gh release list -R millsks/oci-hermit -L 1 --json tagName -q '.[0].tagName'
gh release download $tag -R millsks/oci-hermit -p '*-win-64.zip' -p SHA256SUMS
$zip = Get-Item oci-hermit-*-win-64.zip
$want = (Select-String -Path SHA256SUMS -Pattern $zip.Name -SimpleMatch).Line.Split(' ')[0]
if ((Get-FileHash $zip -Algorithm SHA256).Hash -eq $want) { 'OK' } else { 'MISMATCH' }
Expand-Archive $zip -DestinationPath .

Use osx-arm64 on Apple silicon and osx-64 on an Intel Mac:

tag=$(gh release list -R millsks/oci-hermit -L 1 --json tagName -q '.[0].tagName')
gh release download "$tag" -R millsks/oci-hermit -p '*-osx-arm64.tar.gz' -p SHA256SUMS
shasum -a 256 --ignore-missing -c SHA256SUMS
tar -xzf oci-hermit-*-osx-arm64.tar.gz

Use linux-64 on x86-64 and linux-aarch64 on arm64:

tag=$(gh release list -R millsks/oci-hermit -L 1 --json tagName -q '.[0].tagName')
gh release download "$tag" -R millsks/oci-hermit -p '*-linux-64.tar.gz' -p SHA256SUMS
sha256sum --ignore-missing -c SHA256SUMS
tar -xzf oci-hermit-*-linux-64.tar.gz

gh release list takes the newest release, pre-releases included; gh release download with no tag takes the Latest release instead. Each tab checks the download against SHA256SUMS before unpacking it; anything but OK means a damaged or different file.

If the download never finishes. On some managed networks a browser download from the releases page stalls, going back and forth between 0 and 1 byte and resuming without end. GitHub serves the files from a second host, release-assets.githubusercontent.com, through short-lived links, and a proxy or scanner that holds the file back until it has seen all of it can outlast the link. Download it on another machine and copy it across (a USB stick or a file share is fine), then check it with SHA256SUMS as above. The folder needs nothing from the internet to run. To see what the network is doing, curl.exe -L -v -o oci-hermit.zip <link to the file> prints each step.

You now have an oci-hermit folder. The commands below run from the folder that contains it.

docs.title: 2. Check it
docs.text:
WindowsmacOSLinux 
.\oci-hermit\oci-hermit.exe version
.\oci-hermit\oci-hermit.exe machine info
.\oci-hermit\oci-hermit.exe machine boot

./oci-hermit/oci-hermit version
./oci-hermit/oci-hermit machine info
./oci-hermit/oci-hermit machine boot

./oci-hermit/oci-hermit version
./oci-hermit/oci-hermit machine info
./oci-hermit/oci-hermit machine boot

version prints the version and the control protocol the host speaks:

$ oci-hermit version
oci-hermit 0.2.0 (control protocol 1.4)

machine info lists both emulators with accel tcg, both guests, the defaults run uses, where images are stored and how many there are, and which registry logins it found. Each path says whether it came from a setting or was found beside oci-hermit. On a Mac with Apple silicon it looks like this (paths shortened):

$ oci-hermit machine info
oci-hermit 0.2.0 (control protocol 1.4)
host: macos/aarch64, so images default to linux/arm64

emulator (QEMU, software CPU only):
  bundle:     /Users/me/oci-hermit/qemu (found beside oci-hermit)
  x86_64:     QEMU 11.1.3 (oci-hermit-qemu-4), accel tcg
  aarch64:    QEMU 11.1.3 (oci-hermit-qemu-4), accel tcg

guest (kernel and agent each sandbox boots):
  x86_64:     /Users/me/oci-hermit/guest/x86_64 (kernel 2.9 MB, agent 1.3 MB, found beside oci-hermit)
  aarch64:    /Users/me/oci-hermit/guest/aarch64 (kernel 5.9 MB, agent 1.2 MB, found beside oci-hermit)

sandbox defaults for run:
  cpus:       1 (--cpus)
  memory:     512 MiB for a stored image (its layers are disks); twice the size of one run from a file, plus 256 MiB (--memory)
  network:    none: no egress; -p (127.0.0.1 only) is not implemented yet
  run dir:    /var/folders/kb/…/T/oci-hermit (a sandbox-* folder per run: initramfs, console.log, qemu.log)

image store (pull, load):
  path:       /Users/me/Library/Application Support/oci-hermit/images (the platform default)
  images:     none yet; created by the first pull or load

registries (pulls happen on the host, never in the sandbox):
  auth files: searched in this order; the first with a login for the registry is used
    1. [not set]   $REGISTRY_AUTH_FILE
    2. [not set]   $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/containers/auth.json
    3. [not found] /Users/me/.config/containers/auth.json
    4. [found]     /Users/me/.docker/config.json
  plain http: none (OCI_HERMIT_INSECURE_REGISTRIES)

machine boot starts a sandbox and stops it again, a self-check of QEMU, the kernel and the agent:

$ oci-hermit machine boot
booting an aarch64 sandbox; console log: /var/folders/kb/…/T/oci-hermit/sandbox-12655-1794883275062816000/console.log
agent ready after 0.3s (control protocol 1.4)
guest powered off; sandbox stopped

Add --arch x86_64 or --arch aarch64 to try the other guest.

docs.title: Put it on your PATH
docs.text:
To type oci-hermit without the folder in front, add the folder to your PATH:

WindowsmacOSLinux

For this PowerShell window only:

$env:Path = "$PWD\oci-hermit;$env:Path"

For good, for your account only (no admin rights needed); open a new window afterwards:

[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "$PWD\oci-hermit;" + [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "User"), "User")

For this terminal only:

export PATH="$PWD/oci-hermit:$PATH"

For good, add the same line, with the full path instead of $PWD, to ~/.zshrc.

For this terminal only:

export PATH="$PWD/oci-hermit:$PATH"

For good, add the same line, with the full path instead of $PWD, to ~/.bashrc (or your shell's startup file).

The rest of the documentation assumes you did.

docs.title: 3. Run an image
docs.text:
oci-hermit run public.ecr.aws/docker/library/debian:bookworm-slim sh -c 'uname -a; cat /etc/debian_version'
oci-hermit run -it public.ecr.aws/docker/library/debian:bookworm-slim bash

The first run pulls the image, because it is not stored yet. The second one finds it:

$ oci-hermit run public.ecr.aws/docker/library/debian:bookworm-slim sh -c 'uname -a; cat /etc/debian_version'
Unable to find image 'public.ecr.aws/docker/library/debian:bookworm-slim' locally
5b6c2c6cbc90: pulled (468 B)
2d66c782e484: pulled (28.1 MB)
Digest: sha256:ec8534cda2cb30f29f44f23e135297af7a1496f2990fd8e4e84aa36b081a757a
Linux (none) 6.18.63-oci-hermit-2 #1 SMP 2026-11-10 18:07:06 UTC aarch64 GNU/Linux
12.15

uname -a shows oci-hermit's Linux kernel, whatever your host is. In the shell, type exit to leave.

The same commands work in PowerShell. For -it, Windows Terminal works best.

Other ways in:

oci-hermit pull alpine                          # Docker Hub names work; anonymous pulls there are rate-limited
oci-hermit run alpine cat /etc/os-release
oci-hermit run -u nobody alpine id              # as another user than the image's
oci-hermit run --platform linux/amd64 alpine uname -m   # the other architecture
oci-hermit load -i app.tar                      # from `docker save` or an OCI layout, offline
oci-hermit run ./my-oci-layout sh               # an OCI layout directory or .tar, without storing it

Pulls happen on the host. The sandbox itself never gets network access.

docs.title: Private registries
docs.text:
Log in once, then pull and run as usual:

oci-hermit login registry.example.com          # asks for the user name and password
oci-hermit pull registry.example.com/team/app:1.4
  • login checks the user name and password with the registry before it saves anything, so a typo is reported straight away. With no registry it logs in to Docker Hub.
  • In scripts and CI, pass the password on stdin rather than as an argument, where other users could see it: echo "$TOKEN" | oci-hermit login -u me --password-stdin ghcr.io. Registries such as GHCR take an access token as the password.
  • The login is stored where Podman stores it ($REGISTRY_AUTH_FILE, else $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/containers/auth.json, else ~/.config/containers/auth.json), readable by you only. Podman and skopeo use it too, and logins you already made with podman login or docker login work in oci-hermit without logging in again. machine info lists every auth file it reads and the one login writes.
  • oci-hermit manifest inspect registry.example.com/team/app:1.4 shows which platforms the image has, and their digests and sizes, without pulling it.
  • oci-hermit logout registry.example.com removes the login; logout --all removes them all.
  • More, including tokens for GHCR, GitLab and Harbor: Pull from a private registry.
  • Registry certificates are checked against your operating system's trust store, so a company certificate authority that IT installed works. A CA that is not installed, or a client certificate the registry asks for, goes in a folder for that registry, ~/.config/containers/certs.d/<host:port>/, as Podman and Docker keep them: see a registry with its own CA.

Set OCI_HERMIT_TIMINGS=1 to see how long each phase of a run took. Booting dominates; on CI hosts a shell is ready in 1 to 6 seconds (see Performance and limits).

run -d starts a container in the background and prints its ID; oci-hermit logs -f <name> follows its output and oci-hermit stop <name> stops it. run refuses the flags that are not implemented yet (-p, -v, --pod) instead of ignoring them. The roadmap says when they come.

docs.title: Managing images
docs.text:
The image commands work as in Podman and Docker. They only touch the image store, so they need no sandbox:

oci-hermit images                                 # or `image ls`; -q for IDs, --digests, --no-trunc
oci-hermit tag alpine mine/alpine:test            # another name for the same image
oci-hermit inspect alpine                         # config, layers and names as JSON
oci-hermit image history alpine                   # the steps that built it
oci-hermit image exists alpine && echo stored     # exit 0 if stored, 1 if not
oci-hermit save -o alpine.tar alpine              # every platform stored; --platform for one
oci-hermit rmi mine/alpine:test                   # removes the name; blobs go when nothing uses them
oci-hermit image prune                            # images loaded without a name; -a for every image
oci-hermit system df                              # how much space the store uses
  • Names and IDs: images go by their full name (docker.io/library/alpine:latest; alpine means the same) or by their image ID, the first few characters of which are enough. run takes the same names and IDs.
  • Platforms: an image pulled for both platforms shows up once per platform. rmi and tag act on every platform under the name.
  • Moving images: save writes the format Docker 25 and later write: an OCI image layout with a manifest.json beside it. oci-hermit load, docker load, podman load and skopeo all read it, so it carries images to another machine with no registry in between.
  • One at a time: rmi and image prune refuse to run while another pull, load or run is reading the store, so they never delete an image that is in use. Try again when it has finished.

Manage the image store walks through them, and Move images between machines covers save and load.

docs.text:
What Windows macOS Linux Pulled and loaded images %LOCALAPPDATA%\oci-hermit ~/Library/Application Support/oci-hermit $XDG_DATA_HOME/oci-hermit or ~/.local/share/oci-hermit Each sandbox's logs %TMP%\oci-hermit\sandbox-* $TMPDIR/oci-hermit/sandbox-* $TMPDIR/oci-hermit/sandbox-* (or /tmp)

docs.title: If it will not start
docs.text:
WindowsmacOSLinux

"Windows protected your PC", or a blocked file: the browser marked the download (the Mark of the Web). Unblock the folder, if your organisation allows it:

Get-ChildItem -Recurse .\oci-hermit | Unblock-File

gh downloads are not marked.

"cannot be opened because the developer cannot be verified": the browser quarantined the download. Remove the mark:

xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine oci-hermit

Release binaries will be signed (#39).

"permission denied" on a file that is executable: your home directory may be mounted noexec. Check:

findmnt -no OPTIONS --target ~

machine boot times out: the console log in the sandbox's folder (above) shows how far the guest got. Security software that inspects QEMU can slow it down a lot; give it longer with --timeout 600.

Troubleshooting covers more. On a managed (company) device, check that running an emulator is allowed first, and see Running without admin rights for what it needs and a checklist.

docs.title: Development builds
docs.text:
Every successful CI run on main also publishes the same folder for each host, built from that commit. GitHub keeps these for 14 days, and only signed-in GitHub users can download them. With gh:

run=$(gh run list -R millsks/oci-hermit -w kernel.yml -b main -s success -L 1 --json databaseId -q '.[0].databaseId')
gh run download "$run" -R millsks/oci-hermit -n oci-hermit-osx-arm64   # or -win-64, -osx-64, -linux-64, -linux-aarch64

On Windows this leaves the oci-hermit folder; elsewhere it leaves oci-hermit-<host>.tar.gz to unpack. In a browser: the Guest kernel workflow, the newest run, Artifacts.

docs.title: Building from source
docs.text:
For working on oci-hermit itself. You need pixi, which installs per user.

git clone https://github.com/millsks/oci-hermit
cd oci-hermit
pixi run cargo build --release -p oci-hermit        # target/release/oci-hermit

On Windows, pixi's Rust links with Microsoft's linker, so Visual Studio Build Tools with the "Desktop development with C++" workload must be installed.

The emulator and guest are separate builds:

Piece Build Where QEMU bundle pixi run -e qemu-build qemu-build, writes qemu/out Linux and macOS; Windows builds under MSYS2 (.github/workflows/qemu.yml) Guest kernel pixi run -e kernel-build kernel-build <arch> guest/out/<arch> Linux only, natively per architecture Guest agent pixi run -e agent agent-build Linux only, natively per architecture

You can also take any of them from a CI run instead (oci-hermit-qemu-<host> from the QEMU bundle workflow, sandbox-<arch> from the Guest kernel workflow), or take the whole package above and replace only the binary.

Point a source build at them with two settings, or copy them next to the binary in the package layout:

export OCI_HERMIT_QEMU_DIR=$PWD/qemu/out                 # contains bin/qemu-system-*
export OCI_HERMIT_GUEST_DIR=$PWD/guest/out/sandbox       # contains <arch>/kernel, hermit-agent and crun
target/release/oci-hermit machine info

CONTRIBUTING.md covers the development workflow.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: This page describes what oci-hermit does today, and marks what is planned. The full design, including the parts not built yet, is in the design document.

docs.title: The short version
docs.text:
Each oci-hermit run is one small virtual machine, started for that command and powered off when it ends:

  1. On the host, oci-hermit finds the image: a local OCI layout or .tar, else an image in its store, else it pulls the image from the registry. Every manifest, config and layer is checked against its sha256 digest.
  2. It turns each of the image's layers into a read-only EROFS disk, once per layer (later runs reuse them), works out the user to run as from the image's own /etc/passwd on those disks, and writes an initramfs with the guest agent as /init. Nothing is mounted on the host and nothing needs privileges. (An image run straight from a file has its files put in the initramfs under /rootfs instead.)
  3. It starts the bundled QEMU as a normal child process, with a software CPU (-accel tcg), no network device, and the layer disks attached read-only, and boots oci-hermit's own Linux kernel with that initramfs.
  4. In the guest, the agent runs as PID 1. It moves its root off the initramfs onto a tmpfs (so crun can pivot_root later), mounts /proc, /sys, the cgroup filesystem and /dev, says it is ready, and waits for instructions on a private serial channel.
  5. oci-hermit sends the command and the disks' serial numbers. The agent mounts each disk read-only and stacks them with overlayfs on /rootfs, under a writable layer in the guest's memory that is thrown away with the sandbox, so nothing the command writes reaches the disks. It writes an OCI runtime bundle for the command (its user, environment, working directory and terminal) and starts it in a container with crun: its own PID, mount, IPC, UTS, network and cgroup namespaces, Docker's default capabilities, a read-only /sys and only the usual devices. The agent relays the container's input, output and exit code.
  6. When the command exits, oci-hermit asks the agent to power off, and exits with the command's exit code.

docs.title: Components
docs.text: oci-hermit components The host tool's modules, the QEMU helper process with its control port and serial console, and the guest VM with its kernel, hermit-agent as PID 1, and the command running in a crun container as the image's user. A dashed box lists the planned parts: a seccomp profile, networking, bind mounts and an OS sandbox around QEMU. HOST · your user account, no root, no admin $ oci-hermit run -it IMAGE CMD images store, .tar or dir QEMU bundle qemu-system-* guest dir kernel + agent oci-hermit · Rust host tool cli.rsclap; Docker-style commands main.rsdispatch; run; machine boot, info registry.rspull on the host; logins load.rsload -i: docker save, OCI store.rsimage store (OCI layout), lock images.rsimages, rmi, inspect, tag, save image.rsmanifest per arch; sha256 checks rootfs.rsapply layers in memory users.rsUser from the image's /etc/passwd qemu.rslocate + verify the bundle guest.rskernel + agent per arch initramfs.rsnewc cpio, no privileges supervisor.rsQEMU argv, Sandbox, protocol initrd.cpio /init + /rootfs console.log serial console qemu.log QEMU stderr $TMPDIR/oci-hermit/sandbox-<pid>-<ns>/ stdin / stdout pipes · NDJSON -initrd logs QEMU helper · separate GPL-2.0 process -accel tcg -nodefaults -no-user-config -display none virtio-serial port org.oci-hermit.control chardev stdio, signal=off serial console ttyS0 / ttyAMA0 chardev file → console.log guest VM · microvm (x86_64) / virt (aarch64) Linux 6.18 LTS kernel tinyconfig + fragments, no modules hermit-agent · PID 1 (/init) · static glibc • mounts /proc, /sys, /dev, /dev/pts, /run, /tmp • signalfd (TERM, INT, CHLD) + poll on the control port • Framer: lines ≤ 64 KiB; bad input gets an error reply • one Run per sandbox; relays I/O; reaps children • never exits: sync, then reboot(POWER_OFF) crun container on /rootfs · own pid, mnt, ipc, uts, net, cgroup ns container command crun run --bundle /run/oci-hermit · Docker's capabilities -t: pty from crun's console socket · otherwise 3 pipes PID 1 of its namespace, as the image's User, or -u Run PLANNED · not in the code yet M3 Docker's default seccomp profile in containers (#102) M4 libslirp NIC, restrict=on; -p on 127.0.0.1 only (#26, #27) M5 9P server over virtio-serial; mounts ro by default (#30–#33) M7 OS sandbox around QEMU: seccomp, App Sandbox, AppContainer (#38) Today the VM has no network device. The green arrows are the control channel. oci-hermit holds QEMU's stdin and stdout as an anonymous pipe pair, QEMU's -chardev stdio connects them to the virtio-serial port, and the agent finds the port through /sys/class/virtio-ports. Nothing on the filesystem or the network can reach it. QEMU must never print to stdout, so its diagnostics go to qemu.log. Registry pulls, logins and digest checks all happen in the host tool; the guest never sees a registry or a credential. Part What it is Host tool oci-hermit, one Rust binary. The only process you start. It reads images, talks to registries, builds the initramfs and supervises QEMU. QEMU The bundled emulator (qemu/ in the package), started as a separate process. oci-hermit builds it itself, with only the two guest targets and no hypervisor accelerators, and refuses any other QEMU: its --version must be exactly 11.1.3 (oci-hermit-qemu-4) and it must offer the tcg accelerator. See Building QEMU. Guest kernel Linux 6.18 LTS, built by the project from tinyconfig plus a short list of options. x86_64 guests use QEMU's microvm machine; aarch64 guests use virt. See Building the guest. Guest agent hermit-agent, a static Rust binary that runs as PID 1. It never exits: on a shutdown request or any fatal error it syncs and powers the VM off. Container runtime crun 1.30, built statically by the project with json-c, libseccomp and libcap. The agent hands it an OCI runtime bundle per command. Control protocol Newline-delimited JSON over the virtio-serial port org.oci-hermit.control, at most 64 KiB a line. Version 1.4.

docs.title: What happens when you run
docs.text:
Sequence of oci-hermit run -it Prepare on the host: choose the architecture, locate QEMU, find or pull the image with digest checks, locate the guest, apply the layers and resolve the user, write the initramfs. Boot QEMU, then the Hello and Ready handshake. Run and Started, a loop of Stdin and Output, Exited. Then Shutdown and ShuttingDown, and the guest powers off. PREPARE BOOT COMMAND STOP youterminal oci-hermitmain + supervisor host filesbundle, guest, store QEMU (TCG)helper process hermit-agentPID 1 commandcrun container run -it IMAGE CMD arch: --platform, else the host's (then the other one, with a warning) qemu::locate $OCI_HERMIT_QEMU_DIR, then the install layouts beside oci-hermit open_image a path, else a stored name or ID, else pulled; every blob checked against its digest verify, guest::locate "11.1.3 (oci-hermit-qemu-4)", tcg; <arch>/kernel, hermit-agent and crun rootfs(): layers in order; whiteouts, opaque dirs; ".." refused; User from /etc/passwd initrd.cpio = agent as /init + /dev/console + /rootfs; RAM = 256 MiB + 2 x image (min 512) spawn qemu-system-<arch>; stdin/stdout piped, stderr → qemu.log boot kernel, exec /init mounts, open port, "ready" Hello {version: [1,4]} Ready {version: [1,4]} major must match; host waits up to 120 s raw mode (-t on a terminal); stdin reader thread (-i) Run {argv, env, cwd, tty, user, layers, hostname} bundle; crun run, as the user Started {pid} within 60 s loop until exit stdin bytes Stdin {data} (base64, ≤ 16 KiB raw) pty / pipe output Output {stream, data} stdout / stderr exit → SIGCHLD, reap Exited {code} Shutdown ShuttingDown within 30 s, else QEMU is killed sync; reboot(RB_POWER_OFF) power off; QEMU exits exit with the command's code (125 if oci-hermit itself fails) Green: host to guest. Blue: guest to host. Without -i, the host sends StdinClosed right after Started; with -i it sends it when your stdin reaches end of file. With a terminal (-t), all output arrives as stdout and the terminal stays open. The terminal size is sent once, in Run; resizing the window afterwards is not passed on yet. Set OCI_HERMIT_TIMINGS=1 to print how long prepare, boot, command and stop took.

The host side of this is split in two processes. run does the preparing, then starts the container's monitor, a background oci-hermit __monitor of its own (as Podman's conmon; there is no daemon). The monitor takes the container's running lock, starts QEMU (whose lifetime is tied to the monitor's), does the handshake, Run and Shutdown, appends the output to the container's log and records the exit code. run talks to it over a local channel, a Unix socket in the data folder that only you can open or a named pipe on Windows, in the same kind of JSON lines: it attaches, gets Booted, Started, the output and Exited, and sends your stdin. Without -d the monitor stops the sandbox if run goes away; with -d, run prints the container's ID after Started and returns, and logs reads the log while stop asks the monitor over the same channel to send the container's stop signal (Signal, protocol 1.6, which the agent passes on with crun kill) and to power the sandbox off if it has not ended in time. kill and Ctrl-C at a foreground run send Signal too. exec asks it to start another command in the container: the monitor sends the agent Exec (protocol 1.5) with a process number, the agent runs it with crun exec, and that command's input, output and exit code travel tagged with its number, to that exec alone.

docs.title: Isolation
docs.text:
The security boundary is the emulator process. Guest code never runs directly on your CPU: QEMU translates every instruction, and the guest can touch only the devices QEMU gives it. The layers, outermost first:

Layer Today Planned OS sandbox around QEMU None yet. QEMU runs as you, with your file access. seccomp and Landlock on Linux, App Sandbox on macOS, an AppContainer or low-integrity token on Windows (#38). Process lifetime QEMU ends when oci-hermit does: -run-with exit-with-parent=on on Linux and macOS, a kill-on-close Job Object on Windows. Software CPU TCG only. The bundle is built without KVM, HVF, WHPX or Xen, and any other QEMU is refused. Device model -nodefaults: one serial console and one virtio-serial port. No network card, disks, USB, display or sound. Read-only layer disks (#16), one restricted network card (#26), a file channel for bind mounts (#30). Network Sealed. No network device at all: no way out and no way in. libslirp with restrict=on (#26); -p bound to 127.0.0.1 only, even when 0.0.0.0 is asked for (#27); an egress test suite (#28). Control channel Anonymous pipes, no socket or file. Lines are capped at 64 KiB, anything that is not a message is refused, and every wait has a timeout: the host treats the guest as untrusted. Image input Every manifest, config and layer is checked against its sha256 digest when it is pulled, stored and read. Paths that climb out with .. are refused, device nodes are skipped. Signature verification with cosign or notation (#42). Inside the guest A crun container: its own PID, mount, IPC, UTS, network and cgroup namespaces (no user namespace), Docker's default capabilities, masked and read-only kernel paths, a device allow-list, run as the image's User (or -u). The VM stays the main boundary. Docker's default seccomp profile (#102). Host code Rust, with unsafe code denied in the host crates; cargo deny checks advisories and licences; the QEMU and kernel sources are pinned by sha256. Code-signed Windows and macOS releases (#39).

docs.title: No network, on purpose
docs.text:
The sandbox has no network device. A command that tries to reach anything fails:

$ oci-hermit run public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20 wget -q -T 5 -O- http://example.com
wget: bad address 'example.com'

Pulls happen in the host tool, so the guest never sees a registry, a credential or a route out. An image that downloads things when it starts fails here, which shows it is not self-contained. Published ports, bound to 127.0.0.1 only, are planned (#27); outbound access is not planned at all.

docs.title: The image store
docs.text:
Pulled and loaded images live in one OCI image layout in your data folder (see Configuration). Blobs are shared between images and written only after their digest checks out. Each image is an entry in the layout's index.json, named by its full reference (docker.io/library/alpine:latest) and its platform; an image loaded without a name goes by its image ID.

pull, load and run share the store and can run side by side. rmi and image prune delete blobs, so they need the store to themselves and refuse to start while another oci-hermit is reading it.

docs.title: The control protocol
docs.text:
One JSON object per line, tagged by type. A different major version is refused; a newer minor version only adds messages or fields.

{"type":"hello","version":[1,2]}
{"type":"run","argv":["sh"],"env":["PATH=/usr/bin:/bin","TERM=xterm-256color"],"cwd":"/","tty":true,"rows":40,"cols":120}
{"type":"output","stream":"stdout","data":"aGkK"}
{"type":"exited","code":0}
Direction type Since Meaning host to agent hello 1.0 First message on the channel, with the host's protocol version. host to agent shutdown 1.0 Sync filesystems and power the guest off. host to agent run 1.1 Start one command: argv, env, cwd, tty, and the terminal's rows and cols. user (uid, gid, groups) since 1.2. One per session. host to agent stdin 1.1 Bytes for the command's stdin, base64, at most 16 KiB raw per message. host to agent stdin_closed 1.1 The host's stdin reached end of file. agent to host ready 1.0 Reply to a compatible hello. agent to host shutting_down 1.0 Reply to shutdown, before the power-off. agent to host error 1.0 A refused or failed message. agent to host started 1.1 The command started, with its PID. agent to host output 1.1 Output, base64, on stdout or stderr. With a terminal everything is stdout. agent to host exited 1.1 The exit status, or 128 plus the signal that killed the command.

The host sends a user only to an agent that speaks 1.2 or later, because an older agent would ignore it and run the command as root. oci-hermit version prints the protocol version the host speaks.

docs.title: The QEMU command line
docs.text: Argument Why -accel tcg Software CPU emulation only. Never KVM, HVF, WHPX or Hyper-V. -nodefaults -no-user-config -display none -no-reboot The smallest device set, no host config files, no display. A guest reboot or panic ends QEMU. -machine microvm -cpu Haswell-v4,… x86_64 guests. The agent's static glibc needs an x86-64-v3 CPU; qemu64 would stop it with SIGILL. -machine virt -cpu max aarch64 guests. -m <MiB> -smp <cpus> Memory and CPUs: see Performance and limits. -run-with exit-with-parent=on Linux and macOS only. On Windows a Job Object does the same job. -chardev file,… -serial chardev:console The guest console goes to console.log, for people; oci-hermit never parses it. -chardev stdio,…,signal=off and a virtserialport named org.oci-hermit.control The control channel on QEMU's stdin and stdout. signal=off, so a byte is never taken as Ctrl-C. -append "console=ttyS0 panic=-1 tsc_early_khz=1000000" or "console=ttyAMA0 panic=-1" The kernel command line. The x86_64 guest's clock runs at a fixed 1 GHz on every host, and the kernel is told so. -drive …,readonly=on and -device virtio-blk-device,serial=layerN per layer The image's layer disks, read-only, found by the agent by serial number. No network device.

docs.title: What changes later
docs.text:
• A seccomp profile (#102), as Docker applies by default.
  • Networking (#26 to #29) and bind mounts (#30 to #34), with the defaults described in oci-hermit, Docker and Podman.

docs.title: Running without admin rights
docs.text: oci-hermit is meant for machines where you cannot install Docker or Podman: no admin rights, no hypervisor, no WSL. This page says what it needs from the machine, what CI proves on every change, and how to check a locked-down (managed) device that CI cannot reproduce.

docs.title: What oci-hermit needs
docs.text:
Nothing that requires elevation. A run:

  • starts the bundled QEMU as a normal child process, always with -accel tcg (a software CPU), so KVM, Hyper-V (WHPX) and Apple's Hypervisor framework are never used and need not be enabled;
  • reads the image, kernel and agent from wherever oci-hermit is installed, and never writes there;
  • writes the sandbox's initramfs and logs under your temp directory (TMPDIR, or TMP on Windows), in oci-hermit/sandbox-*;
  • talks to the guest over QEMU's stdin and stdout only: no sockets, no network, no listening ports;
  • on Windows, puts QEMU in a Job Object so it ends when oci-hermit does. Any user can create one.

It installs no driver, service, kernel extension or network adapter, and changes no system setting.

docs.title: What CI proves
docs.text:
Every change runs the hosts job in .github/workflows/kernel.yml on five kinds of host (Windows x64, macOS on Apple silicon and Intel, Linux x64 and arm64), each with an x86_64 and an aarch64 guest. After the usual checks, each job:

  1. creates a new account with no admin rights:
  2. Windows: a local account in the Users group only. The job checks it is not in Administrators (S-1-5-32-544) and runs at medium integrity, so nothing is elevated.
  3. macOS: a standard account. The job checks it is not in the admin group and cannot use sudo.
  4. Linux: a new account in no sudo, adm, wheel, kvm, docker or lxd group. The job checks it cannot use sudo, and takes /dev/kvm away from everyone but root first.
  5. installs oci-hermit, the QEMU bundle, the guest and a Debian image in a folder the account cannot write to;
  6. runs oci-hermit run debian.tar sh -c '...; exit 7' as that account and checks the output and the exit code.

The job summary shows the account's identity, its groups and the command's output. That covers the "no admin rights" part on stock Windows, macOS and Linux.

docs.title: What CI cannot prove
docs.text:
GitHub's runners are not managed devices. Organisations lock machines down with tools that CI does not have, and any of them can stop oci-hermit even though it needs no admin rights:

  • Application allow-listing: AppLocker or App Control for Business (WDAC) on Windows; Santa or an MDM profile on macOS; fapolicyd on Linux.
  • Endpoint protection: Microsoft Defender attack surface reduction rules, or another EDR agent that blocks or quarantines unknown binaries, or kills a process that generates code at run time (QEMU's TCG does).
  • Downloaded-file checks: SmartScreen and the Mark of the Web on Windows, Gatekeeper and quarantine on macOS. Release binaries will be signed (#39); until then expect these to complain.
  • Mount options: a home or temp directory mounted noexec on Linux.

The checklist below is for trying oci-hermit on such a device. Results from real managed devices are tracked in #63.

docs.title: Checklist for a managed device
docs.text:
Use your normal account, with no elevation and no help from IT. Record what you see at each step: the exact message, and any notification from the security software. Stop at the first step that fails; the later steps depend on it.

Before you start, check that this is allowed. Running an emulator may go against the intent of a policy that blocks Docker or Podman, even though it needs no admin rights. See When to use oci-hermit.

docs.title: Every operating system
docs.text:
• Download and unpack the release archive into a folder in your home directory. Note any warning from the browser or the operating system.
  • Start it: oci-hermit version prints the version and the control protocol version.
  • Check the bundled QEMU: oci-hermit machine info lists both emulators with accel tcg.
  • Boot a sandbox: oci-hermit machine boot prints agent ready after …s and then guest powered off.
  • Run an image: oci-hermit run debian.tar sh -c 'echo hello; exit 7' prints hello, and the exit code is 7 (echo $?, or echo %ERRORLEVEL% in cmd).
  • Use a terminal: oci-hermit run -it debian.tar bash gives a prompt. Type ls / and exit.
  • Check the timing: with OCI_HERMIT_TIMINGS=1 set, run prints how long each phase took. A boot much slower than in Measured start times can mean security software is inspecting QEMU.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
• Mark of the Web: if the archive came from a browser, check whether SmartScreen blocks oci-hermit.exe or qemu-system-*.exe, and whether unblocking (file Properties, "Unblock") is allowed.
  • Allow-listing: if AppLocker or App Control is on, note whether it blocks oci-hermit.exe, the QEMU executables or their DLLs. The Event Viewer logs under Applications and Services Logs > Microsoft > Windows > AppLocker or CodeIntegrity name the blocked file.
  • Defender: check Windows Security > Protection history for blocks or quarantines after each step.
  • Location: if the first try was blocked, try again from a folder IT allows for tools, if there is one.
  • Console: run oci-hermit run -it debian.tar bash in Windows Terminal and in the older console host. Check that arrow keys, Ctrl-C and resizing behave.

docs.title: macOS
docs.text:
• Gatekeeper: if the archive came from a browser, check whether macOS refuses to open the binaries, and whether System Settings > Privacy & Security > Open Anyway is offered or hidden by your organisation.
  • Quarantine: check whether xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine <folder> is allowed. If it is, retry.
  • Allow-listing: note any Santa or MDM message naming oci-hermit or qemu-system-*.
  • Endpoint protection: note any alert about a process writing executable memory. QEMU generates code at run time.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
• noexec mounts: run findmnt -no OPTIONS --target ~ and findmnt -no OPTIONS --target "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}". noexec on your home blocks the binaries. oci-hermit only reads from the temp directory, so noexec there is fine.
  • Policy: if run fails with "permission denied" on a binary that is executable, check fapolicyd, SELinux (ausearch -m avc -ts recent) or AppArmor (journalctl -k | grep apparmor) for a denial.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text: Add the results to #63, or open a new issue for each blocker. Include the operating system and version, the security software if you know it, the step that failed, and the exact message. Leave out anything your organisation treats as confidential, such as host names, policy names or internal paths.

docs.title: Performance and limits
docs.text: oci-hermit emulates the guest's CPU in software. That is what lets it run without a hypervisor or admin rights, and it is also why it is slower than Docker. It is meant to answer "does this image work", not "how fast is it".

docs.title: Start time
docs.text:
Starting a sandbox takes about a second on a recent laptop, and 2 to 6 seconds on GitHub's hosted runners. Booting dominates. Set OCI_HERMIT_TIMINGS=1 to see the breakdown of any run:

$ OCI_HERMIT_TIMINGS=1 oci-hermit run public.ecr.aws/docker/library/debian:bookworm-slim bash -ic exit
timings: prepare 0.35s, boot 0.63s, command 0.05s, stop 0.03s, total 1.06s
  • prepare: find the image, build any layer disk it does not have yet (once per layer), read the user from them, write the initramfs. For an image run from a file, apply its layers into the initramfs, which grows with its size.
  • boot: start QEMU, boot the kernel, wait for the agent to be ready.
  • command: start the command and wait for it to exit.
  • stop: power the guest off.

Measured with oci-hermit run debian.tar bash -ic exit (Debian 12 slim), a release build and one vCPU; each row is the run with the median total out of three:

Host Guest Prepare Boot Command Stop Total Apple M4 Mac, macOS 26.2 aarch64 0.31s 0.58s 0.05s 0.02s 0.96s Apple M4 Mac, macOS 26.2 x86_64 0.29s 1.09s 0.05s 0.03s 1.45s GitHub ubuntu-24.04-arm (Linux arm64) aarch64 0.37s 1.40s 0.09s 0.02s 1.88s GitHub ubuntu-24.04-arm (Linux arm64) x86_64 0.34s 3.75s 0.11s 0.02s 4.22s GitHub ubuntu-latest (Ubuntu 26.04, x64) aarch64 0.49s 1.46s 0.11s 0.02s 2.08s GitHub ubuntu-latest (Ubuntu 26.04, x64) x86_64 0.41s 2.41s 0.13s 0.02s 2.98s GitHub windows-latest (Windows Server 2025, x64) aarch64 0.70s 1.43s 0.11s 0.02s 2.26s GitHub windows-latest (Windows Server 2025, x64) x86_64 0.52s 2.80s 0.16s 0.04s 3.54s GitHub macos-latest (macOS 26, Apple silicon) aarch64 0.49s 2.35s 0.12s 0.09s 3.04s GitHub macos-latest (macOS 26, Apple silicon) x86_64 0.50s 2.93s 0.14s 0.03s 3.61s GitHub macos-15-intel (macOS 15, Intel) aarch64 0.96s 4.91s 0.24s 0.06s 6.17s GitHub macos-15-intel (macOS 15, Intel) x86_64 0.61s 3.32s 0.19s 0.04s 4.17s

The CI rows come from the hosts job in kernel.yml, which records the same runs in every job summary. Hosted runners are small shared VMs, so they are slower and noisier than a laptop. An x86_64 guest boots more slowly than an aarch64 one on every host except the Intel Mac. More detail is in the design document.

A boot much slower than these on similar hardware often means security software is inspecting QEMU as it generates code; see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Running time
docs.text:
Once started, everything the command does runs on the emulated CPU. Expect it to be roughly 5 to 20 times slower than native, depending on the work and the host. As an indication: a shell loop counting to a million took 2.5 seconds in the Apple M4 Mac's own /bin/sh, and about 12 seconds in Alpine's sh in either guest (time inside the sandbox):

$ oci-hermit run --platform linux/arm64 public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20 \
    sh -c "time sh -c 'i=0; while [ \$i -lt 1000000 ]; do i=\$((i+1)); done'"
real    0m 12.05s
user    0m 12.04s
sys 0m 0.00s
Work What to expect An interactive shell, small scripts Responsive. A web frontend or backend answering test requests Fine for smoke tests (once published ports arrive, #27). Compiling, large data loads, test suites that are CPU-bound Many times slower than native. Out of scope; run them on a real container runtime. Timing-sensitive tests May be flaky.

docs.title: Memory and CPUs
docs.text:
Default Change with CPUs 1 run --cpus N, machine boot --cpus N Memory for run 512 MiB for a stored image; twice the size plus 256 MiB for one run from a file run -m 2g (at least 64m) Memory for machine boot 512 MiB machine boot --memory 1024 (MiB)

The memory is the guest's RAM, which QEMU reserves on your machine. An image from the store (pulled or loaded) runs from read-only disks, one per layer, so 512 MiB does whatever its size; what the command writes is kept in that RAM until the sandbox stops. An image run straight from a file (run image.tar), or one with more than 20 layers, travels in the initramfs and is unpacked in the guest's RAM instead, so it gets twice its size plus 256 MiB.
