If a command runs out of memory, raise -m. More CPUs help commands that use several threads; booting does not get faster.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• One container per sandbox. Each run boots its own VM for one container, in the foreground or with -d in the background; exec runs more commands in it, but not more containers.
  • No network. No outbound access at all, by design, and no published ports yet (#27).
  • No bind mounts yet (#33). Put what the command needs in the image, or pass it on stdin with -i.
  • Image size. A stored image's layers become disks, once each, so the first run of a large image takes a moment longer and later ones do not. An image run straight from a file is read into memory and copied into the initramfs: fine for a few hundred MB, slow for multi-GB images. load it first to run it from disks.
  • Layer compression. Plain and gzip layers. zstd layers are not supported yet.
  • Platforms. linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 only.
  • Terminal. The terminal size is sent when a -t command starts; resizing the window afterwards is not passed on.
  • Inside the guest each command runs in a crun container with Docker's defaults, but with no seccomp profile yet (#102) and no resource limits beyond the VM's size.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Start with these two commands. Most problems show up in one of them, with the reason:

oci-hermit machine info
oci-hermit machine boot

machine info says what oci-hermit found and where; machine boot boots a sandbox with no image involved. If both work, the problem is with the image or the command. Every error oci-hermit prints starts with oci-hermit:.

docs.title: Where the logs are
docs.text:
Each run and machine boot gets its own folder under the run dir that machine info shows:

OS Run dir Windows %TMP%\oci-hermit\sandbox-<pid>-<time> macOS $TMPDIR/oci-hermit/sandbox-<pid>-<time> Linux $TMPDIR/oci-hermit/sandbox-<pid>-<time>, or under /tmp
  • console.log: the guest's console, the kernel's boot messages and the agent's hermit-agent: … lines. It shows how far the guest got.
  • qemu.log: QEMU's own messages.
  • monitor.log: for a run, what the container's monitor (the background oci-hermit that keeps its sandbox) could not do, such as listen for commands or record how the container ended.

machine boot prints the console log's path as it starts, and an error from a sandbox names both files. The newest folder is the last run. oci-hermit does not delete these folders; remove old ones when you no longer need them.

docs.title: It will not start at all
docs.text:
WindowsmacOSLinux

"Windows protected your PC" (SmartScreen), or the file is blocked. A browser marks what it downloads with the Mark of the Web, and SmartScreen warns about unsigned programs that carry it. Release binaries will be signed (#39). Until then, unblock the folder, if your organisation allows it:

Get-ChildItem -Recurse .\oci-hermit | Unblock-File

Or download with gh run download (see Getting started), which does not mark files.

"This app has been blocked by your system administrator", or nothing happens: application control (AppLocker, App Control for Business) or endpoint protection blocked oci-hermit.exe, qemu-system-*.exe or one of QEMU's DLLs. The Event Viewer, under Applications and Services Logs > Microsoft > Windows > AppLocker or CodeIntegrity, names the blocked file, and Windows Security > Protection history shows Defender's blocks. This needs your IT department; see Running without admin rights.

"cannot be opened because the developer cannot be verified", or "is damaged". Gatekeeper refuses unsigned programs downloaded with a browser, which marks them as quarantined. Release binaries will be signed (#39). Until then, remove the mark from the folder:

xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine oci-hermit

Or download with gh run download, which does not set it. If System Settings > Privacy & Security has no Open Anyway button and xattr is not allowed, your organisation manages this; see Running without admin rights.

"Permission denied" on a file that is executable. Your home directory may be mounted noexec:

findmnt -no OPTIONS --target ~

If the options include noexec, unpack oci-hermit somewhere that allows programs to run. noexec on the temp directory is fine: oci-hermit only reads from there. If the mount is not the cause, check for a policy denial: fapolicyd, SELinux (ausearch -m avc -ts recent) or AppArmor (journalctl -k | grep apparmor).

docs.title: QEMU or the guest is missing
docs.text:
oci-hermit: no bundled QEMU found; looked in …/libexec/oci-hermit/qemu …/qemu (set OCI_HERMIT_QEMU_DIR to a bundle built by qemu/build.sh)

The qemu/ folder is not beside oci-hermit. Keep the package's folder together: the binary, qemu/ and guest/. Copying only oci-hermit(.exe) somewhere else breaks this. To keep them apart, set OCI_HERMIT_QEMU_DIR and OCI_HERMIT_GUEST_DIR (Configuration).

oci-hermit: no x86_64 guest kernel, agent and crun found; looked in … (set OCI_HERMIT_GUEST_DIR to a directory with x86_64/kernel, x86_64/hermit-agent and x86_64/crun)

The guest for that architecture is missing, or it is one from before 0.3 without crun. machine info shows which ones were found. A guest that is too old to run containers is refused with the guest agent speaks control protocol 1.3 and cannot run containers; it needs 1.4 or later: use the guest/ folder that came with this oci-hermit.

A message saying a QEMU is not the bundled QEMU means the folder holds some other QEMU. oci-hermit runs only the bundle it was built for, from the same package or CI run.

docs.title: The boot times out or is very slow
docs.text:
machine boot waits 120 seconds for the agent by default, and so does run. A timeout ends with the agent did not answer within …s and the paths of both logs.

  1. Look at the end of console.log. If the kernel's messages stop early, the guest is stuck or very slow; if the last line is hermit-agent: ready …, the agent started and something on the host side failed.
  2. Try the other guest: oci-hermit machine boot --arch aarch64 or --arch x86_64.
  3. Give it longer: oci-hermit machine boot --timeout 600. If it then boots, the machine is just slow, or something is slowing QEMU down (next section).

QEMU exited before the agent answered means QEMU stopped; qemu.log says why.

docs.title: It is much slower than expected
docs.text: Compare a boot with the measured start times. Endpoint protection often inspects programs that generate code as they run, which QEMU does all the time, and that can make it many times slower. Look for alerts from your security software naming qemu-system-*. Running oci-hermit from a folder IT has allowed, or asking IT for an exclusion, is the fix; there is nothing to change in oci-hermit.

docs.title: Registry errors
docs.text:
Message What to do pulling the manifest of …: error sending request for url (https://…) The registry cannot be reached: check the name, the network and the proxy. … invalid peer certificate … The system does not trust the registry's certificate. If the registry uses your company's own CA, put that CA in the registry's certs.d folder: see a registry with its own CA. … (the registry may want a client certificate: …) The registry asks for a client certificate (mutual TLS). Put it and its key in the registry's certs.d folder: see client certificates. … has no matching ….key A client certificate in a certs.d folder is missing its key (or the other way round). Copy both. pulling the manifest of …: 401 … (no login for … was found …) No login was found for that registry. Check the auth files in machine info and log in. See Pull from a private registry. … the token server … answered 401 or 403 DENIED The login was refused, or it cannot see this repository. pulling the manifest of …: 404 MANIFEST_UNKNOWN or NAME_UNKNOWN Wrong repository or tag, or your login cannot see it. toomanyrequests or rate exceeded The registry is throttling you; Docker Hub limits anonymous pulls. oci-hermit already retried four times. Log in, wait, or use a mirror such as public.ecr.aws/docker/library/… for official images. … does not match its digest: the image is corrupt or has been altered A blob did not hash to its digest, so nothing was stored. Try again; if it repeats, something between you and the registry is changing the data.

A run with an image that is not stored tries to pull it first (Unable to find image '…' locally). For an image you loaded from a file, check the name with oci-hermit images, including the platform: asking for a platform the store does not have also leads to a pull.

docs.title: The command fails to start
docs.text:
Message What it means the agent refused: starting <cmd>: executable file not found in $PATH The image has no such program. Small images have sh, not bash. user "<name>" is not in the image's /etc/passwd The image's User, or -u, names a user the image does not have. Use a number (-u 1000:1000) or a user it does have. the image has no entrypoint or command, and none was given Give a command after the image name. -p/--publish is not supported yet (#27); run it without -p/--publish The flag is planned, not implemented; the same for -v and --pod. the container's control socket … would be longer than the 103 bytes a socket path may have Linux and macOS: the data folder is too deep for the socket a container's monitor listens on. Set OCI_HERMIT_DATA_DIR to a shorter folder. the container's monitor stopped before it was ready: … The background oci-hermit that runs the container could not start it; the rest of the message, or monitor.log, says why. the container name "<name>" is already in use by container … A kept container has that name. Remove it (oci-hermit rm <name>), or choose another name; --rm stops runs from keeping their containers. container <name> is not running From exec: it runs commands only in a running container. Start one with run -d. the guest agent speaks control protocol 1.4, which has no exec; it needs 1.5 or later The container was started with an older guest/ folder. Use the one that came with this oci-hermit, and start the container again. --memory 10m: use e.g. 512m or 2g, at least 64m -m needs a size with a unit, at least 64 MiB. unsupported --platform … Only linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 run.

All of these make run (or exec) exit with 125.

docs.title: A container will not stop or go away
docs.text:
Message What to do container <name> is running; stop it first … oci-hermit stop <name>, or oci-hermit rm -f <name>. stop takes 10 seconds The command ignores SIGTERM, as a PID 1 without a handler does (sleep, many shell scripts), so stop waits out its time and then kills it. Use stop -t 0, handle SIGTERM in the command, or give the image a StopSignal it handles. the container's guest agent is too old to pass signals on … The container was started with a guest/ folder from before 0.3: kill can only send KILL to it, and stop kills it at once. Start it again with the guest that came with this oci-hermit. could not stop container <name>: cannot reach its monitor: … The container's monitor is not answering. Find it (ps aux \| grep __monitor, or Task Manager on Windows: an oci-hermit.exe whose command line ends with the container's ID), end it, and its QEMU stops with it. The container then shows as Exited (unknown) and rm removes it.

On Windows, id=$(oci-hermit run -d …) and other pipes from a run -d do not finish while the container runs, because its monitor inherits the pipe (#105). Redirect the output to a file instead: oci-hermit run -d … > id.txt.

A run without -d takes its container down with it: closing the terminal or killing that run (kill -9) stops the container, which then shows as Exited (137). Ctrl-C does not: it is passed on to the command, which may ignore it (see run). Use -d for a container that should keep running.

docs.title: The image store is busy
docs.text:
oci-hermit: the image store is in use by another oci-hermit (a pull, load or run); try again when it has finished

rmi and image prune delete blobs, so they wait for no one: they refuse while another oci-hermit is reading the store. Let the other command finish and run them again. If no other oci-hermit is running, check for a stuck process (Task Manager, or ps aux | grep oci-hermit).

docs.title: The command cannot reach the network
docs.text: That is by design: the sandbox has no network device, and nothing turns it on. Put what the command needs into the image beforehand. See How it works.

docs.title: Asking for help
docs.text: Open an issue with the output of oci-hermit version and oci-hermit machine info, the command you ran, the full error, and the end of console.log and qemu.log. Leave out anything your organisation treats as confidential. A security problem goes through the security policy instead.

docs.title: When to use oci-hermit
docs.text: oci-hermit is a development and testing tool. It runs a real OCI image on a machine where Docker and Podman are not an option, at the cost of speed. It does not replace the container runtime you deploy to.

docs.title: What it is good for
docs.text:
• Testing the image you will ship. It runs the exact OCI image you deploy: the same bytes, filesystem, entrypoint, command and environment. "Does it start, does the shell work, does the app answer on its port" get real answers.
  • Machines you are not allowed to change. Everything runs as your own user: no root, no admin rights, no kernel driver, no hypervisor, no WSL. The guest runs on an emulated CPU (QEMU TCG), so nothing needs enabling in the firmware or in Windows features.
  • Strong isolation. The boundary is a whole virtual machine, stronger than a container's namespaces. The guest has no network path out, and you reach it only through ports you publish on 127.0.0.1.
  • Other architectures. An arm64 image runs on an x86-64 machine and the other way round. Docker's cross-architecture support uses the same emulation.

docs.title: Where it differs from production
docs.text:
• Speed. Expect roughly 5–20 times slower than native, and slower again when emulating x86-64 on arm64. It answers "does it work", not "how fast is it". Timing-sensitive tests may be flaky.
  • Kernel. Images run on oci-hermit's small guest kernel, not your production hosts' kernel. Most applications never notice. Anything that depends on particular kernel features, cgroup limits or system calls may behave differently.
  • Runtime. oci-hermit run starts the command with crun, a real OCI runtime, with Docker's defaults inside a small VM. It still does not behave exactly like Docker, Kubernetes or your cloud's container service: no seccomp profile yet (#102), no resource limits beyond the VM's size.
  • Deliberate defaults.
    • There is no outbound network at all, so an application that needs to reach the internet fails here and works in production.
    • Bind mounts are read-only unless you add :rw.
    • Published ports bind to 127.0.0.1 only.

docs.title: Recommendations
docs.text:
• Keep a real gate before you deploy. Use oci-hermit for the inner loop. Run the final validation, such as integration tests or a staging deploy, on a real container runtime, for example a Linux CI runner with Docker or Podman.
  • Check your organisation's policy. If Docker and Podman are blocked on your machine on purpose, running a virtual machine emulator may go against that policy even though it needs no admin rights. Get it approved; do not treat "no admin needed" as permission.
  • Build images elsewhere, for now. oci-hermit runs images but does not build them yet. pixi-oci builds and pulls images without Docker, and writes the OCI archives oci-hermit runs.

docs.title: Field manual
docs.text:
The command-line reference is organised by command. This part is organised by task: you have something to do, and each page below is a complete walk-through. A page gives the commands in order, shows what success looks like, says what to do when it fails, and links the reference for the details.

You need to… Walk-through get a shell in a public image, or run one command in it Run a public image and get a shell pull from a registry that needs a login, or one behind a company certificate authority Pull from a private registry run an image you have as a file: docker save, podman save, an OCI archive Bring images in without a registry carry images to a machine with no registry access Move images between machines list, rename, inspect and delete stored images, and free space Manage the image store try oci-hermit on a company laptop, and find out what blocks it Run on a managed device run an amd64 image on an arm64 machine, or the other way round Choose a platform

The commands assume oci-hermit is on your PATH (Getting started). They are the same on Windows, macOS and Linux; where the shell differs, both versions are shown. The outputs were captured on a Mac with Apple silicon, so the host's platform is linux/arm64; on an x64 machine it is linux/amd64.

Every guide uses images from public.ecr.aws/docker/library, Amazon's mirror of the Docker official images, because it has no anonymous rate limit. The same images are on Docker Hub under their short names (alpine, debian:bookworm-slim).

docs.title: Manage the image store
docs.text: When: you want to see what is stored, give an image another name, look inside one, or free space. These commands only read and write the store, a folder you own; they need no sandbox and no network.

docs.title: See what is stored
docs.text:
$ oci-hermit images
REPOSITORY                             TAG             IMAGE ID       PLATFORM      CREATED        SIZE
public.ecr.aws/docker/library/debian   bookworm-slim   5b6c2c6cbc90   linux/arm64   12 days ago    28.1 MB
public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine   3.20            bf8527eb54c3   linux/amd64   7 months ago   3.6 MB
public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine   3.20            ab3fe4defd29   linux/arm64   7 months ago   4.1 MB

There is one row per name and platform, newest first. image ls is the same command.

Option Shows REFERENCE only images from that repository, or with that name: oci-hermit images public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine -q, --quiet only the image IDs, one per line, for scripts --digests a DIGEST column with each manifest's digest --no-trunc full image IDs

Names follow Docker: alpine means docker.io/library/alpine:latest, so oci-hermit images alpine lists the Docker Hub image, not one from another registry.

docs.title: Names and IDs
docs.text:
Every command that takes an image takes either a name or an ID:

  • A name, in full (docker.io/library/alpine:latest) or as Docker shortens it (alpine).
  • An image ID, the digest of the image's config, or the first few characters of it, enough to be unique: ab3f. sha256: in front is optional.

An image pulled for two platforms has two IDs under one name. rmi, tag and save act on every platform under a name.

docs.title: Look inside an image
docs.text:
inspect prints details as JSON, close to podman image inspect: the IDs and digests, names, creation time, platform, size, labels, the image's config (entrypoint, command, environment, working directory and so on), its layers and its history. Trimmed:

$ oci-hermit inspect mine/alpine:test
[
  {
    "Id": "sha256:ab3fe4defd29ba6231229a4d41440ac8bde8218e85870e53876277faa24b35c4",
    "Digest": "sha256:45e09956dc667c5eff3583c9d94830261fb1ca0be10a0a7db36266edf5de9e1d",
    "RepoTags": [
      "docker.io/mine/alpine:test"
    ],
    "Created": "2026-04-16T23:53:24.896953537Z",
    "Architecture": "arm64",
    "Os": "linux",
    "Size": 4093973,
    "Config": {
      "Cmd": [
        "/bin/sh"
      ],
      "Env": [
        "PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/bin:/sbin:/bin"
      ],
      "WorkingDir": "/"
    },
    …
  }
]

A name that matches nothing prints oci-hermit: no such image: … on stderr, and inspect exits 1.

image history shows the steps that built the image, newest first, with the size each one added:

$ oci-hermit image history public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20
IMAGE          CREATED        CREATED BY                                      SIZE     COMMENT
ab3fe4defd29   7 months ago   CMD ["/bin/sh"]                                 0 B      buildkit.dockerfile.v0
<missing>      7 months ago   ADD alpine-minirootfs-3.20.10-aarch64.tar.gz…   4.1 MB   buildkit.dockerfile.v0

--no-trunc shows full IDs and commands; -q only the IDs.

image exists says, through its exit code, whether an image is stored; it prints nothing:

macOS and LinuxWindows 
oci-hermit image exists mine/alpine:test && echo stored

oci-hermit image exists mine/alpine:test; if ($LASTEXITCODE -eq 0) { "stored" }

docs.title: Give an image another name
docs.text:
oci-hermit tag public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20 mine/alpine:test

The new name points at the same image, for every platform stored under the old one; nothing is copied. A name without a registry is a Docker Hub name, so this one is docker.io/mine/alpine:test.

docs.title: Remove images
docs.text:
rmi (or image rm) removes names. When nothing uses an image's blobs any more, they are deleted too:

$ oci-hermit rmi mine/alpine:test
Untagged: docker.io/mine/alpine:test
$ oci-hermit rmi public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20
Untagged: public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20
Deleted: sha256:bf8527eb54c3680e728d5b4b383a8ba730d72dae7236fbc8dff97ed6b224a731

The first rmi only removed a name, because the same image was still stored under another one.

Given an image ID, rmi removes that image. If the ID has several names, it asks you to choose, as Docker and Podman do; -f removes them all:

$ oci-hermit rmi ab3f
oci-hermit: image ab3fe4defd29 has 2 names (docker.io/mine/alpine:test, public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20); remove them by name, or use -f to remove them all
$ oci-hermit rmi -f ab3f
Untagged: docker.io/mine/alpine:test
Untagged: public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20
Deleted: sha256:ab3fe4defd29ba6231229a4d41440ac8bde8218e85870e53876277faa24b35c4

A name that matches nothing prints oci-hermit: no such image: …, and rmi exits 1.

docs.title: Free space
docs.text:
system df shows how much the store holds:

$ oci-hermit system df
TYPE         TOTAL   ACTIVE   SIZE      RECLAIMABLE
Images       3       0        35.9 MB   35.9 MB (100%)
Containers   0       0        0 B       0 B

There are no containers yet, so every image counts as reclaimable.

image prune removes images loaded without a name, and any blob nothing uses (for example the layers of an image that was loaded again from a different archive). It asks first; -f skips the question, and -a removes every image, named or not:

$ oci-hermit image prune -f
Total reclaimed space: 100.1 MB
$ oci-hermit image prune -a
WARNING! This will remove all images.
Are you sure you want to continue? [y/N] y
Deleted Images:
untagged: docker.io/mine/alpine:test
deleted: sha256:bf8527eb54c3680e728d5b4b383a8ba730d72dae7236fbc8dff97ed6b224a731
deleted: sha256:ab3fe4defd29ba6231229a4d41440ac8bde8218e85870e53876277faa24b35c4

Total reclaimed space: 7.7 MB

Anything but y or yes leaves the store as it is.

To start again from nothing, oci-hermit image prune -a -f.

docs.title: One at a time
docs.text:
rmi and image prune delete blobs, so they need the store to themselves. While a pull, load or run is reading it, they refuse with:

oci-hermit: the image store is in use by another oci-hermit (a pull, load or run); try again when it has finished

run lets go of the store once it has read the image, so a long-running command does not block them.

docs.title: Where the store is
docs.text: oci-hermit machine info shows the path, how many images it holds and their size. To keep it somewhere else (another disk, or a scratch folder for a test), set OCI_HERMIT_DATA_DIR; see Configuration.

docs.title: Move images between machines
docs.text: When: one machine can reach the registry and another cannot, or you want to hand a colleague the exact image you tested. save on one machine and load on the other carry images across with no registry in between.

docs.title: 1. On the machine with access: pull, then save
docs.text:
Pull every platform the other machine will need. An image pulled for both shows up once per platform:

$ oci-hermit pull public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20
…
Status: pulled public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20 for linux/arm64
$ oci-hermit pull --platform linux/amd64 public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20
…
Status: pulled public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20 for linux/amd64

Optionally give it the name you want it to have on the other side, then save it. save writes every platform stored under the name, unless --platform picks one:

oci-hermit tag public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20 mine/alpine:test
oci-hermit save -o alpine.tar mine/alpine:test
oci-hermit save --platform linux/amd64 -o alpine-amd64.tar mine/alpine:test

Several names can go in one archive: oci-hermit save -o bundle.tar app:1.2 db:16.

The archive is in the format Docker 25 and later write: an OCI image layout, with a manifest.json beside it for older tools. oci-hermit load, docker load, podman load and skopeo (oci-archive:alpine.tar) all read it, and every blob is checked against its digest as it is written.

docs.title: 2. Carry the file across
docs.text:
Any way that keeps the bytes intact: a shared folder, a USB stick, scp. To check it arrived whole, compare a hash on both sides:

macOS and LinuxWindows 
shasum -a 256 alpine.tar

Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 alpine.tar

load checks every blob anyway, so a damaged archive is refused rather than run.

docs.title: 3. On the other machine: load, then run
docs.text:
$ oci-hermit load -i alpine.tar
Loaded image: docker.io/mine/alpine:test (linux/arm64)
Loaded image: docker.io/mine/alpine:test (linux/amd64)
$ oci-hermit run mine/alpine:test cat /etc/alpine-release
3.20.10

Both platforms arrived, and the image keeps its name, so run finds it without going to the registry. A name without a registry is a Docker Hub name, as in Docker, so mine/alpine:test is docker.io/mine/alpine:test.

Carry every platform you will run

If a run asks for a platform the store does not have, oci-hermit tries to pull it. On a machine with no registry access that fails with a network error. Save every platform you need, or name the platform with --platform so the one you carried is used.

docs.title: Into Docker or Podman
docs.text:
The same archive loads into Docker and Podman, which makes it a way to hand an image back to a machine with a normal container runtime:

docker load -i alpine.tar
podman load -i alpine.tar

docs.title: Choose a platform
docs.text:
When: the image you need was built for another architecture than your machine, or it was built for both and you want to test a particular one.

oci-hermit emulates the guest's CPU, so both architectures run on every host: an linux/arm64 image runs on an Intel or AMD PC, and a linux/amd64 image runs on a Mac with Apple silicon or an arm64 Linux machine. Only Linux images run; Windows container images do not.

Platform Also called Guest linux/amd64 x86_64 guest/x86_64, QEMU's microvm machine linux/arm64 aarch64 guest/aarch64, QEMU's virt machine

docs.title: The default: the host's platform
docs.text:
Without --platform, pull and run use your machine's own platform. machine info names it on its second line:

host: macos/aarch64, so images default to linux/arm64

docs.title: Ask for one with --platform
docs.text:
--platform takes linux/amd64 or linux/arm64; run and pull also accept amd64, arm64, x86_64 and aarch64:

$ oci-hermit run --platform linux/amd64 public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20 uname -m
Unable to find image 'public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20' locally
bf8527eb54c3: pulled (612 B)
25f1d6b1951a: pulled (3.6 MB)
Digest: sha256:c64c687cbea9300178b30c95835354e34c4e4febc4badfe27102879de0483b5e
x86_64

The store already held the arm64 variant, so run pulled the amd64 one. Both are now stored, under the same name:

$ oci-hermit images public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine
REPOSITORY                             TAG    IMAGE ID       PLATFORM      CREATED        SIZE
public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine   3.20   bf8527eb54c3   linux/amd64   7 months ago   3.6 MB
public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine   3.20   ab3fe4defd29   linux/arm64   7 months ago   4.1 MB

The same flag works on pull (oci-hermit pull --platform linux/amd64 …) and on save, which then writes only that platform (spelled in full there, linux/amd64). machine boot --arch x86_64 or --arch aarch64 boots either guest without an image.

Any other platform is refused:

$ oci-hermit run --platform linux/riscv64 alpine.tar true
oci-hermit: unsupported --platform linux/riscv64

docs.title: An image built for one platform only
docs.text:
When an image has no variant for your platform and you did not ask for one, run uses the other one, as Docker does, and says so on stderr:

$ oci-hermit run mine/alpine:test uname -m
WARNING: the image has no linux/arm64 variant; running its linux/amd64 variant (choose with --platform)
x86_64

That applies to stored images, to archives and layouts given as a path, and to pulls. With --platform, there is no fallback: oci-hermit runs exactly that platform, or pulls it, or fails.

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text: Every guest is emulated, so neither platform runs at native speed. The difference between them depends on the host: on the hosts measured, an x86_64 guest boots more slowly than an aarch64 one, except on Intel Macs. See Performance and limits.

docs.title: Test the platform you ship
docs.text: If production runs on amd64 servers, test with --platform linux/amd64, even on an arm64 laptop: an image's variants can differ (a missing package, a binary built for one architecture only), and the variant your host would pick is not the one you deploy.

docs.title: Pull from a private registry
docs.text:
When: your images are in a registry that needs a login (GitHub Container Registry, GitLab, Artifactory, Nexus, Harbor, a cloud registry), or in one whose certificate is issued by your company's own certificate authority.

Pulls always happen in the host tool. The credentials never reach the sandbox, and the sandbox has no network.

docs.title: 1. Log in
docs.text:
oci-hermit login ghcr.io

It asks for the user name and the password (the password is not shown as you type), checks them with the registry, and only then saves them:

$ oci-hermit login ghcr.io
Username: your-user
Password:
Login Succeeded!

A wrong password is reported and nothing is saved:

$ oci-hermit login -u your-user ghcr.io
Password:
oci-hermit: login to ghcr.io failed: the registry rejected the user name or password

Most registries (GHCR, GitLab, Harbor, Quay, Artifactory) take a personal access token in place of the password; create one with read access to packages. With no registry, login logs in to Docker Hub.

In scripts and CI, give the password on stdin, never as an argument, where other users on the machine could see it in the process list:

macOS and LinuxWindows 
echo "$GHCR_TOKEN" | oci-hermit login -u your-user --password-stdin ghcr.io

$env:GHCR_TOKEN | oci-hermit login -u your-user --password-stdin ghcr.io

-p (--password) works too, with a warning. The login is stored where Podman stores it (see the table below), readable by you only, so Podman and skopeo use it as well. --authfile <FILE> stores it somewhere else.

To see who you are logged in as, or to log out:

oci-hermit login --get-login ghcr.io     # prints the user name
oci-hermit logout ghcr.io                # removes that login
oci-hermit logout --all                  # removes every login in the file

logout only changes the file login writes. A login made with docker login lives in Docker's own file; logout says so and points you at docker logout.

docs.title: 2. See which logins oci-hermit can find
docs.text:
oci-hermit machine info

The last section lists every place it looks for an auth file, in order, and whether each one exists:

registries (pulls happen on the host, never in the sandbox):
  auth files: searched in this order; the first with a login for the registry is used
    1. [not set]   $REGISTRY_AUTH_FILE
    2. [not set]   $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/containers/auth.json
    3. [not found] /Users/me/.config/containers/auth.json
    4. [found]     /Users/me/.docker/config.json
  login file: /Users/me/.config/containers/auth.json (where login writes)
  plain http: none (OCI_HERMIT_INSECURE_REGISTRIES)
# File Written by 1 $REGISTRY_AUTH_FILE oci-hermit login and podman login when the variable is set, or you 2 $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/containers/auth.json oci-hermit login and podman login on Linux 3 ~/.config/containers/auth.json ($XDG_CONFIG_HOME/containers/auth.json when that is set) oci-hermit login and podman login on macOS and Windows, and on Linux without $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR 4 ~/.docker/config.json ($DOCKER_CONFIG/config.json when that is set) docker login

For each registry, oci-hermit takes the first file that has a login for it, so a login made with oci-hermit login wins over one in Docker's file. On Windows, ~ is your user profile (%USERPROFILE%).

docs.title: 3. Or use a login you already have
docs.text:
Logins made with Podman or Docker work without logging in again. If either is installed (it does not have to be able to run containers), you can log in with it instead:

podman login ghcr.io
# or
docker login ghcr.io

Then pull as usual:

oci-hermit pull ghcr.io/your-org/your-app:1.2

Credential helpers work too. When an auth file names a helper, in credHelpers for one registry or credsStore for all of them, oci-hermit runs docker-credential-<name> get, as Docker does. Docker Desktop's desktop helper, osxkeychain, wincred, pass, ecr-login and the cloud providers' helpers all work, as long as the helper is on your PATH.

Logins that hand out an identity token instead of a username and password (<token> as the username, as az acr login does) are not supported yet. Log in with a username and an access token instead.

docs.title: 4. Or write an auth file yourself
docs.text:
Where oci-hermit login cannot be run interactively and stdin is not an option, write the file it would have written. Most registries accept a personal access token in place of a password; create one with read access to packages.

The login is username:token, base64-encoded:

macOS and LinuxWindows 
printf '%s' 'your-user:your-token' | base64

[Convert]::ToBase64String([Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetBytes('your-user:your-token'))

Put it in a file, under the registry's host name:

{
  "auths": {
    "ghcr.io": { "auth": "eW91ci11c2VyOnlvdXItdG9rZW4=" }
  }
}

Save it as ~/.config/containers/auth.json (where podman login would put it), or anywhere you like and point REGISTRY_AUTH_FILE at it:

macOS and LinuxWindows 
export REGISTRY_AUTH_FILE="$HOME/registry-auth.json"
chmod 600 "$REGISTRY_AUTH_FILE"
oci-hermit machine info

$env:REGISTRY_AUTH_FILE = "$HOME\registry-auth.json"
oci-hermit machine info

machine info now shows [found] next to it. The file holds a secret: keep it readable only by you, and out of version control.

docs.title: 5. Pull
docs.text:
oci-hermit pull ghcr.io/your-org/your-app:1.2

A pull prints each blob as it arrives, then the manifest's digest:

$ oci-hermit pull public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20
ab3fe4defd29: pulled (628 B)
3f26bc2dec0b: pulled (4.1 MB)
Digest: sha256:45e09956dc667c5eff3583c9d94830261fb1ca0be10a0a7db36266edf5de9e1d
Status: pulled public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20 for linux/arm64

Every manifest, config and layer is checked against its sha256 digest before it is stored; a mismatch stops the pull and the image is not stored. Throttling and server errors (429, 502, 503, 504) are retried four times, after 1, 2, 4 and 8 seconds. run pulls a missing image the same way, so oci-hermit run ghcr.io/your-org/your-app:1.2 works too.

docs.title: A registry behind a company certificate authority
docs.text:
oci-hermit checks registry certificates against the operating system's trust store: the Windows certificate store, the macOS keychain, or the system certificates on Linux. A company root certificate that IT has installed on the machine is therefore trusted with nothing more to do.

When it is not installed, and you cannot install it machine-wide without admin rights, give it to oci-hermit for that registry alone. Put the CA certificate (PEM, the text that starts -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----) in a folder named after the registry, host and port as you write them in image names, with a .crt extension:

macOS and LinuxWindows 
mkdir -p ~/.config/containers/certs.d/registry.corp.example:5000
cp corp-root-ca.pem ~/.config/containers/certs.d/registry.corp.example:5000/ca.crt
oci-hermit pull registry.corp.example:5000/team/app:1.4

A folder name cannot hold a : on Windows, so drop it, as Docker does: registry.corp.example:5000 is registry.corp.example5000.

$dir = "$HOME\.config\containers\certs.d\registry.corp.example5000"
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force $dir
Copy-Item corp-root-ca.pem "$dir\ca.crt"
oci-hermit pull registry.corp.example:5000/team/app:1.4

This is the certs.d layout Podman and Docker use, so a folder you already set up for them works too. oci-hermit looks for the registry's folder in these, in order, and uses the first it finds:

  1. $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/containers/certs.d, or ~/.config/containers/certs.d (Podman, yours)
  2. /etc/containers/certs.d (Podman, the whole machine; macOS and Linux)
  3. ~/.docker/certs.d (Docker)
  4. /etc/docker/certs.d on macOS and Linux, %ProgramData%\docker\certs.d on Windows (Docker, the whole machine)

pull --cert-dir DIR and login --cert-dir DIR use the files in DIR instead. A registry's CAs are trusted for that registry only, on top of the system's, never for any other host. machine info lists the folders and what each holds for which registry.

docs.title: A registry that wants a client certificate
docs.text:
Some registries ask for a client certificate (mutual TLS) as well as, or instead of, a login. Put the certificate and its private key, both PEM, in the registry's folder beside its CA, as a .cert and a .key with the same name:

~/.config/containers/certs.d/registry.corp.example:5000/
  ca.crt          the registry's CA (if the system does not trust it already)
  client.cert     your certificate
  client.key      its private key

A .cert without its .key (or the other way round) is an error, so a half-copied setup is reported instead of failing later. On macOS and Linux, keep the key readable by you only (chmod 600 client.key): oci-hermit warns when other users can read it. It never prints a key.

docs.title: A registry over plain HTTP
docs.text:
A local test registry often has no TLS at all. Name it in OCI_HERMIT_INSECURE_REGISTRIES, as host:port, comma separated:

macOS and LinuxWindows 
export OCI_HERMIT_INSECURE_REGISTRIES=localhost:5000
oci-hermit pull localhost:5000/my-app:dev

$env:OCI_HERMIT_INSECURE_REGISTRIES = "localhost:5000"
oci-hermit pull localhost:5000/my-app:dev

Only the registries named there are reached over HTTP; every other one still needs HTTPS.

docs.title: When it fails
docs.text:
Message What it means pulling the manifest of …: error sending request for url (https://…) The registry cannot be reached: a typo in the name, no network, or a proxy. … invalid peer certificate … (if … uses its own CA, put that CA in …) The registry's certificate is from a CA the system does not trust. Add it as above. … (the registry may want a client certificate: …) The registry asked for a client certificate and got none, or one it does not accept. See client certificates. pulling the manifest of …: 401 … (no login for … was found …) No login for this registry was found. Check machine info and the host name the login is filed under. … the token server … answered 401 or 403 DENIED The login was refused, or it cannot see this repository. pulling the manifest of …: 404 MANIFEST_UNKNOWN or NAME_UNKNOWN The repository or tag is wrong, or your login cannot see it. … does not match its digest: the image is corrupt or has been altered A blob did not hash to its digest, so the image was not stored. Try again; if it repeats, something between you and the registry is changing the data.

More in Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Run a public image and get a shell
docs.text: When: you want to look inside an image, try a command in it, or check that it starts, and the image is in a public registry.

docs.title: 1. Check the sandbox works
docs.text:
oci-hermit machine boot

It prints agent ready after …s and guest powered off; sandbox stopped. If it does not, start with Troubleshooting: nothing below works until this does.

docs.title: 2. Run one command
docs.text:
run takes an image reference and a command. If the image is not stored yet, it is pulled first:

$ oci-hermit run public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20 cat /etc/os-release
Unable to find image 'public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20' locally
ab3fe4defd29: pulled (628 B)
3f26bc2dec0b: pulled (4.1 MB)
Digest: sha256:45e09956dc667c5eff3583c9d94830261fb1ca0be10a0a7db36266edf5de9e1d
NAME="Alpine Linux"
ID=alpine
VERSION_ID=3.20.10
PRETTY_NAME="Alpine Linux v3.20"
HOME_URL="https://alpinelinux.org/"
BUG_REPORT_URL="https://gitlab.alpinelinux.org/alpine/aports/-/issues"

The pull messages go to stderr, the command's output to stdout. The next run of the same image finds it in the store and starts at once. Without a command, run runs the image's own entrypoint and command, as Docker does.

oci-hermit exits with the command's exit code, so it works in scripts:

macOS and LinuxWindows 
$ oci-hermit run public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20 sh -c 'exit 7'; echo $?
7

PS> oci-hermit run public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20 sh -c 'exit 7'; $LASTEXITCODE
7

If oci-hermit itself fails (the image cannot be found, the sandbox does not boot), it exits with 125, as Docker does.

docs.title: 3. Get a shell
docs.text:
-i keeps stdin open and -t gives the command a terminal; together they give you an interactive shell:

oci-hermit run -it public.ecr.aws/docker/library/debian:bookworm-slim bash

Type exit (or press Ctrl-D) to leave; the sandbox powers off. Alpine and other small images have sh instead of bash.

  • On Windows, use Windows Terminal for -it; the older console host works but handles keys less well.
  • The terminal size is sent when the shell starts. Resizing the window afterwards is not passed on yet.

docs.title: 4. Pass input in
docs.text:
With -i and no -t, stdin is a pipe, so you can feed a file or another command's output to the container:

macOS and LinuxWindows 
echo 'hello from the host' | oci-hermit run -i public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20 cat

'hello from the host' | oci-hermit run -i public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20 cat

Without -i, the command's stdin is closed at once.

docs.title: 5. Run as another user
docs.text:
The command runs as the image's User, as Docker runs it. -u picks another, by name or number, with an optional group:

$ oci-hermit run -u nobody public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20 id
uid=65534(nobody) gid=65534(nobody)

Names are looked up in the image's own /etc/passwd and /etc/group, so a name the image does not have is an error. -u 1000:1000 works without either file.

docs.title: 6. Give it more room
docs.text:
Each run gets one emulated CPU and 512 MiB of memory: the image's layers are read-only disks, so its size does not matter. For a heavier command, ask for more:

$ oci-hermit run --cpus 2 -m 1g public.ecr.aws/docker/library/alpine:3.20 sh -c 'nproc; grep MemTotal /proc/meminfo'
2
MemTotal:        1020516 kB

See Performance and limits for what to expect from emulation.

docs.title: What it cannot do yet
docs.text:
Every run is a fresh sandbox, and the files a command changed are gone when it ends. run -d keeps a container running in the background: follow it with oci-hermit logs -f, run more commands in it with oci-hermit exec, and end it with oci-hermit stop. These flags are refused with the issue that adds them, rather than ignored:

$ oci-hermit run -p 8080:80 public.ecr.aws/docker/library/nginx:alpine
oci-hermit: -p/--publish is not supported yet (#27); run it without -p/--publish
Flag Issue -p, --publish #27 -v, --volume #33 --pod #35

Each run is kept as a container that oci-hermit ps -a lists with its exit code, until oci-hermit rm removes it; --rm removes it as soon as the command ends. Give it a name with --name. The sandbox has no network, so a command that downloads something fails (see How it works).

docs.title: Bring images in without a registry
docs.text: When: you have an image as a file rather than in a registry you can reach: a docker save or podman save archive someone sent you, an OCI archive from a build, or an OCI layout directory. Nothing here needs the network.

docs.title: What oci-hermit reads
docs.text:
Format Made by Docker archive, old format (manifest.json, config and layer files) docker save before Docker 25, podman save (the default docker-archive format) Docker archive, Docker 25 and later (an OCI layout with a manifest.json beside it) docker save from Docker 25, oci-hermit save, pixi oci build OCI archive (a .tar of an OCI image layout) podman save --format oci-archive, skopeo copy … oci-archive:…, buildah push … oci-archive:… OCI layout directory skopeo copy … oci:<dir>, podman save --format oci-dir, an unpacked OCI archive

The archive must be a plain .tar. Unpack a compressed one first (gunzip app.tar.gz, or tar -xzf into a directory). Layers inside may be plain or gzip; zstd layers are not supported yet.

docs.title: 1. Make the archive
docs.text:
On a machine with Docker or Podman:

docker save -o app.tar registry.example.com/team/app:1.2
# or
podman save -o app.tar registry.example.com/team/app:1.2
# or, an OCI archive
podman save --format oci-archive -o app.tar registry.example.com/team/app:1.2

docker save writes one platform: the one Docker has pulled. Pull the platform you need first (for example docker pull --platform linux/amd64 …). See Choose a platform.

Copy the file to the machine where oci-hermit runs, any way you like.

docs.title: 2. Load it into the store
docs.text:
$ oci-hermit load -i debian.tar
Loaded image: quay.io/lib/debian:bookworm-slim (linux/arm64)
$ oci-hermit images
REPOSITORY           TAG             IMAGE ID       PLATFORM      CREATED         SIZE
quay.io/lib/debian   bookworm-slim   0e1693e99bef   linux/arm64   21 months ago   29.9 MB

load reads every platform in the archive and checks every blob against its digest. The image keeps the name it was saved under, and run finds it by that name, without going to the registry:

$ oci-hermit run quay.io/lib/debian:bookworm-slim cat /etc/debian_version
12.9

Loading the same image again, from either format, replaces its name. The blobs the old copy used stay in the store until oci-hermit image prune removes them; see Manage the image store.

docs.title: 3. An image without a name
docs.text:
An archive or layout with no name in it is stored under its image ID:

$ oci-hermit load -i ./unnamed
Loaded image ID: sha256:ab3fe4defd29ba6231229a4d41440ac8bde8218e85870e53876277faa24b35c4 (linux/arm64)
$ oci-hermit images
REPOSITORY   TAG      IMAGE ID       PLATFORM      CREATED        SIZE
<none>       <none>   ab3fe4defd29   linux/arm64   7 months ago   4.1 MB

Use the ID, or enough of its start to be unique, wherever a name goes, and give it a name with tag:

oci-hermit run ab3f cat /etc/alpine-release
oci-hermit tag ab3f myteam/alpine:3.20

oci-hermit image prune removes images that have no name.

docs.title: Or run it without storing it
docs.text:
run also takes the path of an archive or a layout directory, and reads the image from there. Nothing is copied into the store:

$ oci-hermit run alpine.tar cat /etc/alpine-release
3.20.10
$ oci-hermit run ./layout uname -m
aarch64

This suits a one-off check, or a folder you cannot write to. A path wins over a stored name, so write ./name to be sure a relative path is read as one.

docs.title: When it fails
docs.text: Message What it means … does not match its digest: the image is corrupt or has been altered The file was damaged on the way. Copy it again. the image has no linux/<arch> variant …, a warning from run The archive holds only the other architecture; run uses it anyway. See Choose a platform. an error about a zstd layer The image was pushed with zstd compression. Re-save it with gzip layers, for example with skopeo copy --dest-compress-format gzip.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: Each release's downloads are on its GitHub release page.

The host and guest now speak control protocol 1.3, and oci-hermit refuses an older guest agent. Replace the whole oci-hermit folder; do not copy the new oci-hermit or hrmt over a 0.1.0 install. The image store from 0.1.0 keeps working; layer disks are built into it the first time each image runs.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• run runs a pulled or loaded image from its layer disks, stacked with overlayfs under a writable layer that is thrown away when the run ends, so an image of any size runs in 512 MiB instead of twice its size in memory. An image run straight from a path, or one with more than 20 layers, still goes into memory (#98, #17)
  • Each image layer is built once into a read-only EROFS disk and kept in the store; rmi and image prune remove the disks with their layers, and system df counts them (#97, #16)
  • manifest inspect shows an image's platforms and digests without pulling it (#95, #76)
  • Per-registry CA certificates and client certificates for pull, login and manifest inspect, from Podman's and Docker's certs.d folders or --cert-dir, without admin rights; machine info lists the folders it reads (#94, #86)

docs.title: Bug fixes
docs.text:
• The release's source archive falls back to verified mirrors when a download host fails (#92)
  • The Windows CI package step no longer fails with "Permission denied" (#96)

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
• Getting started shows how to check the Windows download and what to do when a browser download never finishes (#92)
  • The private registry field manual covers registries with their own CA or client certificates (#94)

docs.title: Refactoring
docs.text: • pull uses oci-hermit's own registry client on reqwest instead of oci-client, which drops the unmaintained chrono dependency and its advisory exception (#93, #91)
The first pre-release.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Releases: one download per host with oci-hermit, the hrmt alias, QEMU and both guests, their licenses, and a separate archive with the source of every GPL and LGPL component (#89)
  • login and logout, checked with the registry and stored in Podman's auth.json (#88)
  • Image commands: images (image ls), rmi (image rm), inspect, tag, save, image prune, image history, image exists, system df and info (#85)
  • machine info shows the guest, the defaults run uses, the image store and the registry auth files it reads (#74)
  • run runs an image built for the other architecture when the image has no variant for the host's, with a warning (#72)
  • load -i reads docker save archives (old and Docker 25+) and OCI layouts, offline (#71)
  • pull pulls images from registries, with Podman and Docker logins, and verifies every digest (#70)
  • run runs the command as the image's User, and -u/--user picks another (#68)

docs.title: Development setup
docs.text:
Run pixi run bootstrap once per clone to install the pre-commit and commit-msg hooks.

The development environment is managed with pixi, which provides the Rust toolchain from conda-forge.

pixi run build      # cargo build --workspace
pixi run test       # cargo test --workspace
pixi run fmt        # format
pixi run lint       # clippy -D warnings
pixi run ci         # the full gate: pre-commit, build, check, clippy, coverage >= 90%

Plain cargo works too if you already have a recent stable Rust.

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:

docs.title: Ground rules from the design
docs.text:
• Nothing may require root, admin rights or hardware virtualization.
  • The sandbox never gets egress. Changes that open a path out of the guest need a design discussion first.
  • No unsafe in host-side code without a documented reason.

docs.title: Security policy
docs.text: oci-hermit is a sandbox, so a way out of it is a security problem: guest code reaching the host, the guest reaching the network, a bind mount reaching more than it should, or an image that is run although its digest does not match. So is anything that makes oci-hermit need elevated rights.

docs.title: Reporting a vulnerability
docs.text:
Report it privately through GitHub: Report a vulnerability (Security → Advisories → Report a vulnerability). The report is visible only to the maintainers until an advisory is published.

Please do not open a public issue for a security problem, and please do not disclose it elsewhere before a fix is out. If GitHub's form is not available to you, open a public issue asking for a private channel, with no details in it, and one will be arranged.

What to include: the output of oci-hermit version, the host operating system and architecture, the command you ran, and the smallest image or input that reproduces it. For anything involving a crafted image or archive, attach it or say where to get it. Logs help: each sandbox's console.log and qemu.log (their folder is shown by oci-hermit machine info under run dir).

docs.title: What to expect
docs.text:
Acknowledgment Within 3 business days. This is a small project with one maintainer; if you have heard nothing after that, ping the advisory thread. Assessment Within 10 business days: whether it is in scope, how severe, and a rough fix timeline. Fix and disclosure A fix on main (and in a release, once there are releases), then a published GitHub Security Advisory with a CVE where one is warranted. Credit You are named in the advisory unless you would rather not be. Say which you prefer.

There is no bug bounty.

docs.title: Supported versions
docs.text: None yet: oci-hermit is pre-release. There is no release to support (#39, #40, #41). Fixes go to main, and the CI builds of main are the only builds. Once there are releases, the latest release will be the supported one, and this section will say so.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
In scope: the host tool (crates/oci-hermit), the guest agent (crates/hermit-agent), the control protocol (crates/hermit-proto), the guest kernel configuration, and the way oci-hermit builds and launches QEMU.

A vulnerability in QEMU or Linux itself belongs upstream. Tell us as well if oci-hermit's configuration exposes it (a device or option the sandbox does not need, for example), because that part is ours to fix.

Documented differences from Docker are not vulnerabilities: published ports binding to 127.0.0.1 only, bind mounts being read-only by default, and the guest having no network at all are deliberate. So are the limits of the current release that the documentation states, such as there being no OS sandbox around the emulator yet (#38) and no image signature verification yet (#42).

docs.title: Bundled QEMU
docs.text: oci-hermit runs its own build of QEMU, never one already on the machine. conda-forge has no system-emulation QEMU for macOS or Windows (its Linux packages are user-mode qemu-execve-* only), and distribution builds carry hypervisor accelerators, displays, USB and more that the sandbox does not want.

docs.title: What is built
docs.text:
build.sh builds QEMU 11.1.3 from the release tarball on download.qemu.org, checked against a pinned sha256, with:

  • targets x86_64-softmmu and aarch64-softmmu only
  • --without-default-features: no KVM, HVF, WHPX or Xen, no display, audio, USB, tools, docs or guest agent
  • no debug info, which with GCC (Linux, MinGW) tripled the bundle's size
  • user-mode networking (libslirp) and libfdt from the build environment, with --disable-download so nothing is fetched at build time
  • the version marker --with-pkgversion=oci-hermit-qemu-<revision>

The host tool refuses any QEMU whose --version does not report exactly 11.1.3 (oci-hermit-qemu-<revision>), or that has no TCG accelerator (crates/oci-hermit/src/qemu.rs). Changing the configuration means bumping BUNDLE_REVISION in build.sh and BUNDLE_MARKER in qemu.rs together.

docs.title: Patches
docs.text:
build.sh applies qemu/patches/*.patch to the release sources, in order, before configuring. They are QEMU changes and carry QEMU's license, GPL-2.0-or-later. A change to a patch changes the build stamp and the CI cache keys, so the bundle is rebuilt.

Patch Why 0001-chardev-win-stdio-hold-input-until-the-frontend-can-take-it.patch On Windows, -chardev stdio dropped input bytes the frontend could not take yet, so the host's first control message was lost before the guest opened the port. The patch holds the byte until the frontend accepts it, as the POSIX chardevs do, and stops dropping \r from piped (binary) input. Worth offering upstream. 0002-i386-tcg-tsc-counts-nanoseconds-of-virtual-time.patch Under TCG the x86 guest's TSC followed the host's cycle counter, so its frequency differed by host and the guest kernel had to calibrate it against the PIT. That is slow under emulation and failed on loaded hosts; microvm has no HPET or ACPI PM timer to fall back on, so the guest hung at boot. The TSC now counts nanoseconds of virtual time, 1 GHz everywhere, and the host tool passes tsc_early_khz=1000000.

docs.title: Where each platform's build comes from
docs.text:
Platform Built on Build dependencies from linux-64, linux-aarch64 GitHub-hosted Ubuntu runners conda-forge, via pixi run -e qemu-build osx-arm64, osx-64 GitHub-hosted macOS runners conda-forge, via pixi run -e qemu-build win-64 GitHub-hosted Windows runner MSYS2 UCRT64 (conda-forge has no libslirp for win-64, and QEMU does not build with MSVC), plus qemu.qmp==0.0.6 from PyPI, which MSYS2 does not package

.github/workflows/qemu.yml builds all five, checks each with oci-hermit machine info, and uploads them as artifacts. Release packaging and signing come later (#39, #40, #41).

docs.title: Bundle layout
docs.text:
bin/qemu-system-x86_64[.exe]
bin/qemu-system-aarch64[.exe]
bin/*.dll                 Windows: the DLLs QEMU loads
lib/                      Linux and macOS: the shared libraries QEMU loads, found through its rpath
share/qemu/bios-microvm.bin   microvm's SeaBIOS
share/qemu/linuxboot_dma.bin  the option ROM SeaBIOS needs to boot a -kernel bzImage
BUNDLE.txt                version, tarball sha256, marker, host

The bundle is relocatable: libraries are found through the binaries' rpath, and the host tool always passes -L <bundle>/share/qemu for firmware, because QEMU's own relocation does not apply to a / prefix.

The host tool looks for the bundle, in order, in $OCI_HERMIT_QEMU_DIR, <prefix>/libexec/oci-hermit/qemu beside a prefix install of oci-hermit, and qemu/ next to the executable.

docs.title: Building locally
docs.text:
pixi run -e qemu-build qemu-build       # Linux or macOS; writes qemu/out
OCI_HERMIT_QEMU_DIR=$PWD/qemu/out pixi run cargo run -p oci-hermit -- machine info

docs.title: Guest
docs.text: What runs inside the sandbox VM. The guest only ever sees QEMU's virtual devices, so it is the same on every host.

docs.title: Kernel
docs.text:
kernel/build.sh builds Linux 6.18.63, the newest longterm (LTS) release on kernel.org, from the release tarball, checked against a pinned sha256 (from kernel.org's signed sha256sums.asc). No distribution kernels.

The configuration is make tinyconfig with two fragments merged over it by scripts/kconfig/merge_config.sh, then make olddefconfig. The build fails if any option a fragment asks for does not end up in the final .config.

Fragment What it adds kernel/config/common.config printk and earlycon; virtio-mmio with virtio-blk, virtio-net, virtio-console and virtio-rng; 9P with NET_9P_FD (bind mounts over virtio-serial); overlayfs, EROFS, tmpfs, devtmpfs (automounted), proc, sysfs, devpts; IPv4 and IPv6 (so [::] and ::1 work), loopback and unix sockets; mount, PID, net, IPC, UTS and user namespaces; cgroup v2 with the memory, cpu and pids controllers, and cgroup BPF for crun's device rules; seccomp; ELF and #! binaries; initramfs (gzip, zstd) kernel/config/x86_64.config 64-bit, 8250 serial console, CMOS RTC, ACPI and the PCI layer ACPI needs, for QEMU's microvm machine kernel/config/aarch64.config PL011 serial console and PL031 RTC, for QEMU's virt machine

Everything is built in: no modules, graphics, sound, USB, wireless or real-hardware drivers, and no debug info.

The x86_64 kernel has the PCI layer although microvm has no PCI bus. Without it ACPI fails to load ("AE_BAD_PARAMETER, During Region initialization"), so PnP-ACPI never sets up the serial port's interrupt: the kernel's own messages still reach the console, but every write from userspace fails with EIO, which looks like a hung guest (#54).

Architecture Machine Image Console x86_64 microvm (firmware bios-microvm.bin) bzImage, zstd-compressed console=ttyS0 aarch64 virt, -cpu max Image console=ttyAMA0

Builds are reproducible: the build user, host, version counter and timestamp (the release's own) are fixed, and the kernel release string is 6.18.63-oci-hermit-<revision>. Bump KERNEL_REVISION in build.sh when the configuration changes without a new kernel release.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
guest/out/<arch>/bzImage or Image
guest/out/<arch>/config      the final .config
guest/out/<arch>/BUNDLE.txt  kernel version, tarball sha256, release, image and config sha256, compiler

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
Kernels build natively on Linux only (x86_64 on x86_64, aarch64 on aarch64), with the toolchain from the pixi kernel-build environment:

pixi run -e kernel-build kernel-build                       # this machine's architecture, into guest/out/<arch>
pixi run -e kernel-build kernel-build aarch64 guest/out/aarch64

docs.title: Boot test
docs.text:
kernel/boot-test.sh boots a kernel under the bundled QEMU (qemu/README.md) with TCG, no initramfs and no root disk, and passes when the console shows the kernel looking for init (No working init found or Unable to mount root fs). It runs on any host the QEMU bundle runs on, so a kernel built in CI can be tested on macOS too:

pixi run -e qemu-build qemu-build                           # writes qemu/out
bash guest/kernel/boot-test.sh aarch64 qemu/out guest/out/aarch64/Image

.github/workflows/kernel.yml builds both architectures on GitHub-hosted Linux runners, boot-tests each, and uploads the image, config and BUNDLE.txt as artifacts.

docs.title: crun
docs.text:
Each command runs in a container started by crun. crun/build.sh builds it statically for one architecture, with the libraries it links, all from release tarballs checked against pinned sha256 sums:

Component Version License Why crun 1.30.1 GPL-2.0-or-later (libcrun LGPL-2.1-or-later) the OCI runtime json-c 0.18 MIT crun reads config.json with it libseccomp 2.6.1 LGPL-2.1-only seccomp filters (a profile comes with #102) libcap 2.78 BSD-3-Clause or GPL-2.0-only capabilities

crun is configured without systemd (cgroups are managed through cgroupfs), CRIU, dlopened handlers or a shared libcrun, and linked against the same conda-forge 2.39 sysroot as the agent, so the glibc source in the release's source archive covers both. The build fails unless the binary is static and reports +CAP and +SECCOMP.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
<out>/crun                    the static binary
<out>/licenses/<name>/        each component's license files
<out>/licenses/SOURCES.json   name, version, license and source tarball of each
<out>/CRUN.txt                versions, the binary's sha256, the compiler and crun's feature list

packaging/licenses.py crun <guest-dir> <out> merges the licenses and sources into a guest folder.

docs.title: Building
docs.text:
Natively on Linux only, like the kernel:

pixi run -e crun-build crun-build                           # this machine's architecture, into guest/out/crun-<arch>
pixi run -e crun-build crun-build aarch64 guest/out/crun-aarch64

The host puts crun in the initramfs at /bin/crun. At boot the agent moves its root onto a tmpfs, taking crun along, because crun's pivot_root refuses an initramfs root.
